name: Washington State Standard
title: WA pays $180K to fired head of youth prisons who alleged retaliation
description: Washington state is settling for $180,000 with the former head of the state’s youth prison system after she alleged she was fired for raising concerns about longstanding overcrowding. Felice Upton, then assistant secretary of juvenile rehabilitation at Washington’s Department of Children, Youth and Families, was fired in April 2025, without explanation, afte[...]
text:
A sign and fence at the Green Hill School for juvenile offenders, in Chehalis, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Washington state is settling for $180,000 with the former head of the state’s youth prison system after she alleged she was fired for raising concerns about longstanding overcrowding.
Felice Upton, then assistant secretary of juvenile rehabilitation at Washington’s Department of Children, Youth and Families, was fired in April 2025, without explanation, after five years at the agency. In her role, she oversaw the state’s then-two youth prisons: Echo Glen Children’s Center in Snoqualmie and Green Hill School in Chehalis.
Upton alleged Secretary Tana Senn fired her for being a whistleblower.
During her tenure, conditions became increasingly dangerous in the state’s juvenile detention system, especially at Green Hill School. There, overcrowding contributed to a facility wrought with fights and drugs, as well as more time isolated for the young men held there. Staff shortages undercut programs that tend to make juvenile facilities more appealing than adult prisons. 
A state appellate court last year ruled the overcrowding at Green Hill violated state law.
A scathing state audit also recently found steep staff turnover, though state officials say conditions are improving. 
The crowding came after state lawmakers changed law to send young people convicted of crimes to youth detention instead of adult prison until age 25.

Felice Upton. (Photo provided by Toby Marshall)

Upton also pointed to the closure of Naselle Youth Camp, another juvenile detention center in Pacific County. Upton said she learned of the planned closure on her first day as assistant secretary in 2021. She told agency leaders that Echo Glen and Green Hill couldn’t provide the capacity to make up for the closure, according to a claim Upton filed against the state last year. She reportedly presented proposals to address this, but they were ignored.
Naselle shuttered in 2022. 
A year later, her warnings had become reality, according to her claim. In September 2023, she briefed agency higher-ups, including then-Secretary Ross Hunter, on the unconstitutional treatment of the detained youth and unsafe conditions for staff due to crowding. She continued to warn of the conditions over the next year.
“There were other ways she believed to try to address these issues that would have assured both the youth who are in custody are being dealt with in an appropriate manner and that taxpayer dollars aren’t being wasted,” said Upton’s lawyer, Toby Marshall.
In response, agency leaders downplayed the problems and excluded Upton from key decisions about juvenile detention, Upton alleged. Hunter faced calls for his resignation after transferring 43 young men from Green Hill to an adult prison, and suspending intakes at Green Hill. 
Upton reported she also complained to the governor’s office of toxic work conditions and inequitable treatment of women and employees of color, leading to an investigation. She felt her treatment was retaliation for raising concerns.
Upton reached a $180,000 settlement with the state in late May.
As is customary, the state is not admitting fault as part of the agreement and still disputes Upton’s claims. 
The Department of Children, Youth and Families declined to comment on the settlement. Senn, who became secretary in early 2025, said last year that Upton’s concerns “were in no part a factor in the personnel and organizational changes I made in executive leadership when I joined as the new head of DCYF.”
The final settlement is far from the $4.75 million Upton was seeking last August when she filed her claim for damages with the state, a precursor to a lawsuit filed in court. 
Marshall acknowledged Upton’s case was “challenging,” given her leadership job at the agency was to raise issues, making it hard to show she was a whistleblower.
“We believe in Ms. Upton’s claims, but recognize it would’ve been difficult to prove liability,” Marshall, of the Seattle-based Terrell Marshall law firm, said Wednesday.
Upton declined to comment on the settlement Thursday.
Upton started out at the agency as superintendent at Echo Glen. She was assistant secretary for nearly four years before her ouster. Before that, she worked at the state Department of Corrections, which runs Washington’s adult prison system.
She’s now working as an associate principal at Health Management Associates, focusing on improving criminal justice outcomes.
Jennifer Redman, the former superintendent at Green Hill, replaced Upton as assistant secretary.
Overcrowding has eased with the opening of a smaller facility last year on the grounds of an adult prison in Aberdeen. That detention center, Harbor Heights, acts as a release valve for the overpopulation, taking young men from Green Hill. At the end of July, 182 people were held at Green Hill, the lowest level this year. Its safe operating capacity is 180.
Harbor Heights has seen tumult, as well. The state fired the facility’s first superintendent this spring after an internal investigation into sexual harassment allegations.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota company is tackling nitrogen pollution with ag science in volatile fertilizer market
description: When the U.S. started bombing Iran in February and trade routes bottlenecked, Minnesota farmer Les Anderson watched synthetic nitrogen fertilizer prices skyrocket.  Making the product requires natural gas, a fuel source shipped through the currently blockaded Strait of Hormuz and further threatened by Iranian counterattacks on a major Qatari liquefied natura[...]
text:
Sample rows of corn grow at Minnesota Farmfest in Redwood County, Minnesota Tuesday, Aug. 5, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)When the U.S. started bombing Iran in February and trade routes bottlenecked, Minnesota farmer Les Anderson watched synthetic nitrogen fertilizer prices skyrocket. 
Making the product requires natural gas, a fuel source shipped through the currently blockaded Strait of Hormuz and further threatened by Iranian counterattacks on a major Qatari liquefied natural gas facility. 
So when planting season arrived in the spring, the cost of the fertilizer had nearly doubled from the previous year. 
“You know how electric cars have range anxiety? We farmers have nitrogen anxiety,” Anderson said. 
That’s when Anderson, who previously served as president of the Minnesota Corn Growers Association, leaned on a product he had spent recent years experimenting with at his Cannon Falls corn and soybean farm — one that departs from traditional sources of fertilizer. 
The alternative is made by Pivot Bio, a company selling farmers a self-sustaining, non-synthetic, bacterial source of nitrogen, with the aim to lower the nitrogen levels that are the source of significant water pollution in farm states.
The company moved to Minnesota from California in early 2026. 
Since beginning commercial sales around six years ago, the fertilizer has been used on millions of acres by thousands of farmers, including corn, wheat, cotton and sorghum growers, according to the company. But there’s massive room to grow: The American fertilizer market alone is more than $40 billion at wholesale, according to the International Fertilizer Association. 
Pivot Bio has seen a major increase in sales since international trade began to fragment last winter, according to CEO Chris Abbott, though the company declined to provide any data. 
How does it work?
Abbott characterized the product as bacteria that act like “little nitrogen factories.” 
“Pivot Bio pinpoint a microbe natural to a crop’s specific microbiome with the genetic code for nitrogen fixation, reads a company explainer. “We evaluate billions of ways to edit the microbe’s own genetic code to enable its nitrogen fixation powers.” 
It’s typically applied as a coating on the seed that sticks to the plant as it grows, continuously fertilizing it throughout the process — all without leaching the nitrogen into the ground. 
The new tech helps to shield the environment from the toxic runoff that seeps into the ground when nitrogen is applied to crops in excess. 
And, having a relatively fixed amount of fertilizer throughout the growing season helps to soothe the “nitrogen anxiety” Anderson described. 
“You simply can’t make it through the season if you don’t have enough (nitrogen),” he said.  
In his own trials, Anderson said the product was particularly useful in periods of higher rainfall, when traditional, synthetic nitrogen fertilizers otherwise wash away. It’s even more useful when the price of those fertilizers doubles, he added. 
To reach the same yield, Pivot Bio users are on average applying half the amount of nitrogen compared with synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. Anderson confirmed those results have played out on his own farm. 
‘Don’t bury your head in the sand’
For more than a century, farmers like Anderson have been using synthetic nitrogen fertilizers to allow them to quickly produce higher yields. The material has been used to feed an exploding world population through global hardships, like drought and war.
But synthetics have also been proven to cause severely degraded soil health and widespread water pollution. 
Minnesota for years has seen rising nitrate levels in drinking water sources, which can cause birth defects, blue baby syndrome and cancer. Toxic algal blooms are also becoming more common. Both trends are largely tied to the use of synthetic nitrate fertilizer in large-scale farming operations.
Water pollution has become so severe in Iowa that it’s changing the state’s politics and has become a bipartisan issue. 
Employing incentives to nurture sustainable fertilizing practices has been a growing priority for Minnesota, Department of Agriculture Commissioner Thom Petersen told Abbott during a meeting at the Capitol last month. 
Minnesota has several programs in place to assist farmers in doing so, including the Biofertilizer Innovation and Efficiency Pilot Program, climate friendly agricultural practices incentive payments and the Green Fertilizer Program. 
Still, of the many farmers Anderson has gotten to know over the years, most are apprehensive about new technology, he said. 
Many have been “burned” by ag tech companies claiming to have the “newest and greatest” products, he said. Pivot Bio, which is currently valued at roughly $2 billion, appears to be overcoming that skepticism thus far, with rising fertilizer prices likely to spur further experimentation by farmers. 
He encouraged farmers to optimize their nitrogen use, especially before they are forced to do so by state regulations, leaving one final message for his colleagues: “Don’t bury your head in the sand.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. officials announce disbursement of $122 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund awards
description: Of a total $189 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund awards that Virginia received late last year, $122 million has been allocated so far to various entities around the state, state health officials announced Friday.  The money is meant to hire and retain rural healthcare providers, invest in healthcare technologies and strengthen the industry’s workf[...]
text:
Healthcare payment concept with stethoscope and big money US dollar. (Stock photo by Getty Images)Of a total $189 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund awards that Virginia received late last year, $122 million has been allocated so far to various entities around the state, state health officials announced Friday. 
The money is meant to hire and retain rural healthcare providers, invest in healthcare technologies and strengthen the industry’s workforce in rural areas.
“The ground is shifting under our health care system, and rural communities are feeling that uncertainty in real time,” Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa said in a release announcing the disbursement. “These investments allow us to create stability where we can, innovate where it makes sense, and keep care within reach for the people who need it.”
Various community-based organizations including the Virginia Hospital and Healthcare Association Foundation, are among the first waves of grantees who will use the money to boost remote patient monitoring and rural medical residency slots in hospitals.
“Because rural Virginians have distinct health needs and may face barriers to accessing care close to home, hospitals serving those communities are investing in innovative approaches to care delivery that promote public health and meet the needs of patients and families,” said Julian Walker of the Virginia Hospital & Healthcare Association. “In this environment, the Virginia Rural Health Transformation initiative represents an important opportunity to advance rural healthcare delivery.”
The Virginia Foundation for Community College Education will use the funding to help grow the healthcare workforce.
The Virginia Department of Health, which has regional offices around the state, will invest in maternal care and community paramedicine, especially in areas where obstetrics units have dwindled or disappeared. 
State report finds 13 rural hospitals vulnerable to closure 

The Virginia Department for Aging and Rehabilitative Services also received money in the initial disbursement, to improve integration of care for people who are dual-enrolled in Medicare and Medicaid. 
“There is innovation in rural communities already, now we get to tap into it,” Virginia’s RHTF director Heidi Hertz said in a previous interview.   
Virginia’s millions in grant money come from a $10 billion pool available to states each year for the next five years. 
The fund was created during negotiations over Congress’ reconciliation bill passed this summer and has been hailed by President Donald Trump’s administration as a critical investment in rural health care and means to address longstanding challenges. 
“We think we have an opportunity not just to plug a few of the holes, but to transform in a lasting way the rural health care system in this country,” Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services Administrator Mehmet Oz said in a press call last year. 
Before his term expired, former Gov. Glenn Youngkin submitted an application for the funds, laying the blueprint that Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration is now carrying out. States must spend the money in meaningful ways or risk the federal government clawing some of it back. 
During a conversation earlier in the summer, Figueroa noted an “inherent tension” between celebrating the promise that the rural healthcare funding represents for states alongside the reality of how forthcoming changes stemming from H.R. 1 will further exacerbate long-simmering healthcare issues. 
“We’re kind of dealing with the world as it is, and so we’re managing both of those two realities at any given moment,” he said. 
The reconciliation bill entails major changes to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Congress also did not renew expired Affordable Care Act subsidies. 
With thousands having already lost ACA insurance and several thousand more people at risk of losing Medicaid, the state has invested millions to both comply with H.R. 1 and prevent eligible people from losing coverage. 
As Spanberger announced an executive order this week to build on statewide efforts to prepare for H.R. 1 implementation deadlines, Figueroa assured Virginians the administration would do its best to meet the unique new challenges. 
“What we can promise is disciplined execution. We will communicate early,” he said. “We will tell the truth of what we can and can’t do. We will publish the data, and we will listen when the process is not working and try to fix it.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: ICE detains Coast immigrant working to gain green card
description: Heriberto Reyes-Ochoas, nicknamed Eddie, and his wife Catherine Cool have been married since 2014 and met as teenagers. On Aug. 21, he was detained by a state trooper after a fender bender in Hancock County and how is in an immigration detention center in Louisiana.
text:
Ever since Catherine Cool and Heriberto Reyes-Ochoas married over a decade ago, she has worried about immigration officials detaining her husband. 
Each time Reyes, nicknamed Eddie, drove from their home in Hancock County to work at a marine construction company in Slidell, Louisiana, she felt anxious that he wouldn’t make it back home. 
That fear struck last week when Reyes got into a fender bender about 10 minutes from home in Kiln. Nobody was injured, but the Mississippi Highway Patrol trooper who responded determined Reyes, who emigrated from Mexico 20 years ago, did not have legal immigration status and took him to the local jail.
The 34-year-old spent the weekend there before paying bond to leave Monday, only for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to take him into custody the next day. By Thursday, Reyes was at the Adams County Correctional Center in Natchez facing deportation proceedings. 
“This is like a nightmare come true,” Cool, who is 35 and an American citizen, told Mississippi Today. “But we’re going to do what we can.”
The couple celebrated their 12th wedding anniversary last weekend while Reyes was in jail. She is pregnant with their first child, who is due in January. 
‘He’s here doing the right thing’
In the mid-2000s, when Reyes was a teenager, he and an uncle traveled through Texas and made their way to Mississippi. When his uncle left, Reyes lived with an older woman and her family until he was able to be on his own, Cool said. 
The couple met as teenagers working at a Mexican restaurant in Bay St. Louis. They have been together since 2010 and married four years later. 
Heriberto Reyes-Ochoas, nicknamed Eddie, and his wife Catherine Cool are expecting their first child due in January. They have been married since 2014 and met as teenagers, a few years after Reyes came from Mexico with a family member. Reyes has been going through the process to obtain permanent residency and had been waiting for an interview through a consulate office. Credit: Courtesy of Savannah Corbitt
Reyes has taken steps to secure permanent residency, starting with a petition by an American sponsor which had been approved years ago. Because he did not have lawful entry into the U.S., Reyes has had to seek a green hard through consular processing, said Delaney Mecham, Reyes’ attorney.   
The last step in that process is an interview with the consulate in Mexico. But, his attorney said there are some challenges to that. The U.S. Department of State has paused the visa application process and interviews while Reyes was waiting for one. Any adult who entered the country without authorization and then leaves is subject to a 10-year bar from reentering. Although a waiver has been filed to enable Reyes to go to a consulate interview, Mecham said there is the possibility he wouldn’t be able to return to the U.S. 
“We’re not trying to hide the way he came in,” Cool said. “We’re doing what we’re supposed to do through relief given to people like him through the government, and it still doesn’t seem to help.” 
Reyes does not have a criminal record, according to his wife.
Cool’s sister, Savannah Corbitt, shared Reyes’ story on Facebook Wednesday morning and it has been shared over 500 times. The post directs people to call U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell’s office and the offices of U.S. Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith. People sharing and responding to the post have also suggested contacting Gulf Coast state lawmakers. 
In the post, Corbitt wrote that Reyes has been part of the family for years. They’ve known each other since they were teenagers. He’s held her children when they were young and has shown up for birthdays, family dinners, holidays and other ordinary days, she said.
“If you know Eddie, you know exactly what kind of man he is,” Corbitt wrote. “He is the person who will do anything he can for anyone who needs him. And right now, he needs us.”
Corbitt also started a petition calling for Reyes’ release from detention while his immigration proceedings continue.
What happened?
The day of the minor accident, the trooper told Reyes he had an immigration warrant against him and detained him. They were confused about the warrant because, Cool said, Reyes’ only contact with immigration officials has been through a petition and waiver filed on his behalf through the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. 
Reyes’ detention by the trooper was possible through the 287(g) program, which allows local and state law enforcement to work with ICE. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety signed an agreement last year giving the Highway Patrol and several other divisions authority to enforce federal immigration laws during routine policing. 
Mecham said local and state law enforcement’s willingness to work with ICE has led to children being separated from their parents and two-parent households turning into single-parent ones. 
He said he sees the partnerships as more of a political talking point than a practical benefit for communities. Mecham said a better use of resources would be for local law enforcement to address violent crime and local policing rather than civil immigration matters. The federal government has the resources to address its immigration laws, he said. 
“At a community level, these rules will cause more harm for our community,” Mecham said. 
Once in ICE custody, officers interviewed Reyes at their office in Gulfport and determined he would be detained, his wife said. 
Mecham said he requested ICE release Reyes on personal recognizance or on parole, but that did not happen. 
ICE will likely not grant the bond, Mecham said, even though there is nothing in the record to indicate Reyes is a flight risk or a danger to the community. Reyes has strong incentives to appear in immigration court, Mecham said. He noted that his client is near the end of a lengthy process to obtain a green card, and the life Reyes has built with Cool on the Gulf Coast is another incentive. 
‘He’s willing to fight it’
The Adams County Correctional Center in Adams County, Miss., on March 19, 2026 Credit: Rory Doyle for The New York Times
Cool works in Mecham’s immigration office, and she said she has seen the impact of immigration enforcement and detention on people. Now she is experiencing it.
For the past seven years, Cool has worked in the immigration field and is pursuing a career in immigration law. She graduated from Loyola University New Orleans in May and plans to take the bar exam in February.
Cool visited Reyes when he was still at the jail, but on Wednesday he was transferred from Hancock County. She and family thought he would be taken to a detention center in Louisiana, but on Thursday he called her from the Adams County facility to say he was there. 
He seems upset and doesn’t understand the situation, Cool said. 
His attorney will consider other ways to secure his release, such filing a habeas corpus petition in federal court. 
“He said he’s willing to fight it to try and get out,” Cool said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri labor unions, abortion rights groups turn unlikely alliance into ballot power
description: A coalition of Missouri labor unions and reproductive rights groups announced a $1 million campaign this month aimed at defeating Republican lawmakers who voted to repeal the state’s paid sick leave requirement. Not long ago, such a partnership would’ve seemed unusual and unlikely. But years of organizing — and repeated battles with the Republican-controlled[...]
text:
Missouri labor and reproductive rights groups came together ahead of the August 2026 election to rally against Amendments 4 and 5 (photo submitted).A coalition of Missouri labor unions and reproductive rights groups announced a $1 million campaign this month aimed at defeating Republican lawmakers who voted to repeal the state’s paid sick leave requirement.
Not long ago, such a partnership would’ve seemed unusual and unlikely.
But years of organizing — and repeated battles with the Republican-controlled legislature over abortion rights, worker protections and the initiative petition process — have drawn the movements increasingly close together.
The results have been striking at the ballot box.
In 2018, voters overwhelmingly repealed a right-to-work law passed by lawmakers. In 2020, they expanded Medicaid. Four years later, they approved both abortion rights and a higher minimum wage with paid sick leave.
And this August, unions and reproductive rights groups worked together to help defeat Amendments 4 and 5, proposals dealing with the initiative petition process and elimination of the state income tax.
Now comes another test. In November, Missourians will be asked whether they want to repeal the abortion rights amendment they approved in 2024 and reinstate an abortion ban.
“We’ve tried to figure out in the kind of swing-back that we’ve seen from the legislature,” said Caitlyn Adams, executive director of Missouri Jobs with Justice. “How to not get picked off one-by-one, but stand as a united front against the attacks.”
M’Evie Mead, campaign director for Protect Majority Rule, a committee created to oppose Amendment 4, said by building an “incredibly powerful, interconnected movement of people,” goals like raising the minimum wage and expanding Medicaid eligibility were possible in a state dominated by Republicans. 
“We can win these concrete victories,” she said, “that improve people’s economic and reproductive lives.” 
Clarke Wheeler, a senior policy analyst with the National Women’s Law Center, said labor unions and reproductive rights groups in Missouri have excelled at connecting their issues in a way that resonates with voters. 
Missouri, she said, is a “shining example of the power of cross-movement organizing and what it looks like on the ground in real life.”
 Siloed efforts were futile 

Decades ago, the two movements at times found themselves pitted against each other. 
“The labor unions, back when the Democrats ran the state, had members and constituencies and legislators who were friendly to labor, but unfriendly to reproductive rights,” said Michael Wolff, a former chief justice of the Missouri Supreme Court and dean emeritus at the St. Louis University School of Law. 
Nancy Cross, former vice president of SEIU Local 1, has been part of the conversations mobilizing union workers to support reproductive rights for decades. She moved to Missouri in 2004 to work for the Service Employees International Union, tasked with getting a local St. Louis union back on its feet.
Cross points to 2011 as a pivotal year, as more lawmakers began favoring right-to-work. It was the first time she recalls reproductive rights groups really backing the union fight. 
“They understood from the beginning that if this happens, we’re all in jeopardy,” she said. 
The Missouri Independent 100: Tracking the PACs funding state legislative races

Abortion rights advocates and union increasingly began sitting down together. 
“The enemy of my enemy is my ally, so we began working more with others,” Cross said. “I personally believe in a big tent, that you should bring as many people as you can to your position in order to win, because nobody can really win by themselves.”
But it would take several more years for the partnership between unions and reproductive rights groups to become what it is today. 
“It’s been a really long learning curve that outsiders think happened overnight, but, frankly, they were slogging it out before I got here,” Cross said. “And we’re still slogging it out.” 
Leaders of both movements started meeting on a regular basis. Sometimes the goal wasn’t to reach an agreement on an issue, but rather to agree not to fight one another’s issues.
The most pushback came from Catholic union leaders in St. Louis, Cross recalled. 
“Even if you’re pro-life, the ability to have a choice of whether or not you want to have a child or not, is a right that impacts your work,” she said. “Because maybe you don’t have a lot of benefits for working there. Maybe you don’t have health insurance.”
Then, in 2017, the legislature passed right-to-work. 
“All of a sudden you realize, ‘they’re coming after me, even if I don’t get engaged with this issue,’” Cross said of labor leaders at the time.
 Repro backs labor unions in pivotal moment

By the close of her career as president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Federation of America in 2018, Cecile Richards — whose career began as a labor organizer — had been promoting coalition-building with labor groups on the national level for years. 
Among those paying attention was Mead, who moved to Missouri in 1994 to serve as executive director of NARAL Pro-Choice Missouri (now known as Abortion Action Missouri) before working at Planned Parenthood Advocates in Missouri. 
“Abortion is often used in this state as a wedge issue,” she said. “So moving some of the political attitudes in labor from ‘how could they use abortion as a wedge’ to realizing that their members needed access to reproductive healthcare and viewing the issue as a political tool versus a reality of their members’ lives, that just took conversations and time.” 
So in 2018, with Missourians set to vote on whether to repeal a right-to-work law passed by the legislature the year prior, Mead saw an opportunity for reproductive rights groups to get involved in what she framed as an economic justice fight.
If labor was to ever show up for abortion rights, she said, reproductive rights groups needed to fight alongside labor, too. 
Planned Parenthood announced an official position against right-to-work. The organization sent out 17,000 mailers, 20,000 texts and 150,000 emails to their supporters. 
That August, voters repealed right-to-work with about 67% of the vote.
 Medicaid expansion, paid sick leave and abortion

For years, Michelle Trupiano, who at the time worked on government affairs for Planned Parenthood in Missouri, said she worked largely in a silo and watched as advocates in Jefferson City avoided talking about abortion. The fear of any blowback for supporting abortion rights was real, she said, and immobilizing.
As deals were made in the statehouse, reproductive rights issues were regularly “getting thrown under the bus,” said Trupiano, who now works as executive director of Beacon Reproductive Health Network.
Then in 2020, Trupiano headed a Medicaid expansion coalition, bringing together an unlikely crew of stakeholders that included reproductive rights groups, unions, hospitals and business interests.
“Medicaid expansion really specifically showed what can happen when you build broad-based coalitions to achieve something,” she said of the effort, which ultimately passed with about 53% of the vote. 
Mallory Schwarz, who has served as executive director of Abortion Action Missouri since 2019, oversaw the organization as it committed to backing the Medicaid expansion effort in 2020. But the decision wasn’t without its “growing pains,” she said.
Some members and donors asked why Abortion Action Missouri was investing so much in the Medicaid effort when a fight to overturn a 2019 abortion trigger ban was also brewing.
“Because we know that the people that rely on Medicaid for reproductive healthcare and that the birth control they get from Medicaid or the postpartum support that you can get is as necessary to reproductive health as abortion is,” she told them. 
By the time an effort to increase the minimum wage and guarantee paid sick leave, called Proposition A, was on the ballot four years later, Schwarz said she was no longer getting questions internally about how the issues were connected. 
Andi Phillips speaks at a rally on the Missouri Capitol steps on May 15 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Also on the ballot that year was a citizen-led effort to overturn the state’s abortion ban. Schwarz helped lead a coalition that ultimately succeeded in placing the amendment on the ballot with the goal of protecting the right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability. 
“I think for someone to have someone come to their door and talk about Prop A and abortion in the same breath was maybe a new experience for people,” she said.
Then came the endorsement of the reproductive rights amendment by the Missouri AFL-CIO,  the first time the union took a public stance on abortion rights.
The amendment won with just shy of 52% of the vote. Proposition A won with more than 57% of the vote.
“They’ve done a lot of work to make sure partisan politicalness doesn’t creep in,” Schwarz said of the labor movement’s continued support of reproductive rights. “Attacks on abortion, reproductive health, impact workers more than anyone, really, because whether you can afford to get care often impacts your ability to get that care.”
Adams, with Missouri Jobs with Justice, helped lead the August campaign against attempts by lawmakers to both raise the threshold for changing the state constitution by initiative petition and an effort to eliminate the state income tax. 
This summer, Abortion Action Missouri stood beside Missouri Workers Power and Missouri Jobs with Justice as union and reproductive rights leaders rallied voters across the state against Amendments 4 and 5. 
“There’ve been so many opportunities over the last decade to throw down together,” said Adams. 
That doesn’t mean the coalition agrees on everything.
The work isn’t rainbows and butterflies, Adams said, as they work with union leaders across political ideologies and diverse backgrounds to draw connections between healthcare and economics. 
“The idea that it’s about control, and a voice over your own body and in your own family, goes way further than my opinion of abortions can save people’s lives,” she said, adding: “If we lose one thing, we’re likely to lose another. If we win one thing, we’re likely to be able to win another.”
Demonstrators ordered out of the Missouri House public gallery during a debate on anti-abortion legislation march and chant Wednesday, May 13, 2026, in the Missouri Capitol Building (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Adams grew up in Buckner, a small town about 45 minutes outside of Kansas City. Her father was a Republican. Her mother is a Democrat.
“But when the school didn’t have enough supplies to hand out at the beginning of the year, my dad didn’t care that he was a Republican,” she said. “He was making sure the community came together to make that happen.” 
That memory is her own testament to what Adams believes motivates Missourians, both in their communities and at the ballot box. 
“Missouri can buck the idea that the legislature tries to push, that we need to be divided, that we should be so polarized,” she said. “People really care about their communities and their neighbors, and that can go beyond partisan politics.”
The coalition’s next test comes in November.
Schwarz said recent history gives her hope that Missourians will vote down the proposed abortion ban. 
“Voters don’t want politicians to be able to change the rules.  They want to be able to focus on their families,” she said. “They want to be able to live in a state that’s affordable, and where you can make a living wage, you can live on your paycheck and get the healthcare you need in your community. Those are all really basic, shared values that I think Missourians have. And it’s the politicians that muddy the rest of it.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri says its intoxicating hemp ban is clear. Industry says it’s unconstitutional
description: A federal judge is being asked to decide whether Missouri’s new law banning intoxicating hemp products is clear enough to enforce in November or so contradictory that a constitutional challenge to it should move forward. At the center of the dispute is the question of whether Missouri calls a product legal “hemp” in one part […]
text:
Missouri Hemp Trade Association president Jay Patel speaks during a press conference on the Missouri State Capitol steps April 14 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A federal judge is being asked to decide whether Missouri’s new law banning intoxicating hemp products is clear enough to enforce in November or so contradictory that a constitutional challenge to it should move forward.
At the center of the dispute is the question of whether Missouri calls a product legal “hemp” in one part of state law and illegal “marijuana” in another.
The plaintiffs, led by the Missouri Hemp Trade Association, said in a motion this week that the state has created overlapping definitions, leaving businesses unsure what they can legally sell when the law goes into effect on Nov. 12. They argue the case over House Bill 2641 deserves to be heard in court. 
“Most judges would read [House Bill 2641] and go, ‘What is going on here?’” said Chuck Hatfield, attorney for the plaintiffs. “‘This seems like something we need to at least dig into and figure out.’ And that’s what our clients want is a day in court.”
The state says there’s no contradiction because the law specifically outlines which category controls: if it meets the definition of a hemp-derived cannabinoid product, it’s treated as marijuana. The state asked Judge M. Douglas Harpool of the U.S. District Court Western District of Missouri to dismiss the lawsuit earlier this month. 
The state argues the case is part of a growing nationwide effort by the hemp industry to overturn similar state laws.
“The industry’s playbook is well established,” the motion to dismiss states, citing other federal cases where the challenges against other state legislation regulating intoxicating hemp have failed. 
Plaintiffs hit back in their response this week, saying that Missouri’s law is different from the other states cited. These products will be considered marijuana in Missouri under the new law, they argue, and that’s where the legislation gets “unconstitutionally vague.” 
The federal law distinguishing marijuana and hemp has brought intense debate both in the legislature and courts nationwide since Congress legalized hemp in 2018. 
For Missouri, the lawsuit is the latest episode in a long saga to regulate intoxicating hemp products that, in previous years, has ended with lawmakers throwing their hands up in frustration. 
When Congress legalized hemp in 2018, it opened a door for intoxicating products like hemp-derived THC beverages that are now found in grocery stores and bars throughout the state. 
Congress closed that loophole in November by passing a federal ban that’s set to go into effect Nov. 12. Missouri lawmakers said they intended to mirror that language by a law passed this spring. 
However, plaintiffs argue in the lawsuit that the result is “a single product is simultaneously legal ‘hemp’ and  illegal ‘marijuana.’” 
The state argues in its motion to dismiss that it prevented this scenario because it “enacted provisions to guard against confusion.”
“In other words, to the extent that a hemp-derived cannabinoid meets the statute’s definition of ‘hemp’ and is not included in any of the statute’s exclusions from ‘hemp,’ then the product is not a ‘hemp-derived cannabinoid product’ for purposes of HB 2641’s central mandate,” according to the state’s motion. “It is that simple.” 
The bill, sponsored by Republican state Rep. Dave Hinman of O’Fallon, will prohibit hemp products from containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container, which is among the limits included in a provision in the federal spending bill Congress approved last year.
Even if Congress reverses course and decides to allow the sale of these products, Hinman’s bill would only permit them to be sold in Missouri’s licensed marijuana dispensaries. And if Congress chooses to delay the ban, Missouri would still ban all products, except for intoxicating beverages. 
However, plaintiffs argue beverages are not specifically stated as being exempt.
The law lists types of products that would go into effect if there was a delay, which includes “any solid candy, gummy, chewable product, tablet, capsule, oil, baked good, or other solid edible.” It also includes products “that can be smokable or vapeable in the form of raw plant material, flower, or bud material and that contain any amount of tetrahydrocannabinolic acid.”
Beverages are thought to be allowed because they aren’t on the list of things that would go into effect. However, critics have said other products might be unintentionally exempt because they are not listed here, not just beverages, and the law just creates another loophole. Plaintiffs point to the carve-out clause as further reason the law is “difficult to parse.”
This list has become a bigger focus because Congress is currently considering delaying the federal ban.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Senate approved a measure to fund federal agencies until Dec. 11, and it includes delaying the federal ban on intoxicating hemp THC products until that date. It now goes back to the U.S. House for final approval before heading to the president’s desk.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: Nebraska needs Republicans who will make government work
description: There’s an old saying: You cannot spend your way to prosperity. But you cannot cut your way to prosperity either. And Nebraska is learning that lesson the hard way. Gov. Jim Pillen came into office with a record surplus, and now we are facing a budget shortfall approaching $1 billion, according to the Nebraska Economic […]
text:
The Nebraska State Capitol. Sept. 12, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)There’s an old saying: You cannot spend your way to prosperity. But you cannot cut your way to prosperity either. And Nebraska is learning that lesson the hard way.
Gov. Jim Pillen came into office with a record surplus, and now we are facing a budget shortfall approaching $1 billion, according to the Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board. It’s the result of the governor’s overspending and failure to properly budget and manage the state’s finances.
He has a “my way or the highway” approach to governing that dovetails neatly into his desire to return the Republican Party to being the party of austerity, the party of tax cuts for multinational corporations, the party that attacks and wants to cut Social Security.
Government is not a business; it exists for the common good. But saying otherwise doesn’t justify an overly simplistic tool like an across-the-board 5% cut to state spending, as Governor Pillen has done.
Nebraska is facing a slow-motion repeat of Kansas’ disastrous 2012 tax-cut experiment. Kansas slashed corporate and income taxes on the promise that economic growth would make up the difference. It didn’t. The result was years of crippling deficits, spending cuts and eventually a reversal of much of the tax-cut package.
Our state is already on that path. We handed out massive tax breaks and incentives without building the production, investment and economic growth needed to replace the revenue. Now we’re staring down massive deficits and responding with across-the-board cuts.
If Pillen ran his business the way he has run Nebraska, he would have gone bankrupt years ago.
And that gets to a larger problem with the Republican Party. We have spent too much time arguing about whether government should be bigger or smaller and not enough time asking whether it actually works. Tax cuts and spending cuts became virtues in themselves. But neither tells us whether we are making our country stronger, safer and more prosperous.
That’s what helped create the political environment that produced Donald Trump.
Too many voters heard Republicans talk about tax cuts that seemed to benefit multinational corporations and wealthy interests while telling ordinary Americans that government could not protect their jobs, communities or the programs they had spent their lives paying into. They heard politicians talk about reducing Social Security rather than protecting it for the people who earned it.
Then the 2016 presidential election happened and the political status quo broke.
Voters wanted a government that would fight for them. They wanted safer communities, secure borders, protected American industries and leaders willing to challenge powerful corporations and entrenched interests.
It was a rejection of a version of conservatism that had stopped speaking to its political base.
Nebraska Republicans should learn that lesson rather than trying to reverse it. But that cannot become an excuse to return to the politics that made the GOP irrelevant and doomed until President Trump came along.
We should reject the false choice between bloated government and no government.
The goal should be strong government that understands its responsibilities and performs them exceptionally well. Government should keep communities safe, enforce the law, maintain infrastructure, provide essential services and protect taxpayers from fraud and abuse.
A 5% cut to every agency may reduce spending, but it does not tell us whether the right things were cut. A balanced budget does not prove government is working. A Triple-A credit rating does not tell a Nebraska family whether their community is safer or whether they are receiving value for their taxes.
We need a right-wing party willing to challenge corporate welfare as aggressively as it challenges government waste. It should lower taxes on working families and Nebraska businesses while refusing special favors for politically connected interests. It should believe in law and order while demanding that government actually deliver safe communities.
Most importantly, Republicans should stop being afraid to say that government has legitimate responsibilities.
The answer to bad government is not necessarily less government. Sometimes the answer is better government. The answer to waste is not an arbitrary percentage cut. It is accountability. Government should do what government is supposed to do and do it exceptionally well.
We do not need Republicans who simply promise to make government smaller. Our state needs Republicans who will make government work. That is the Republican future I believe in.

name: WyoFile
title: Legislature could determine the fate of Wyoming’s $13M in Meta settlement funds
authors: Katie Klingsporn and The Associated Press
description:
Under landmark deal, company also commits to several new safety and time-cap features for its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram.
The post Legislature could determine the fate of Wyoming’s $13M in Meta settlement funds appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming will receive more than $13 million from the landmark settlement deal with Meta Platforms over claims its social media sites have harmed children. 
The funds are part of a multistate deal announced Wednesday marking the end of a trial over teen social media addiction. In the legal settlement, Meta agreed to pay a total of $18 billion to nearly every state and strengthen child-safety measures on its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
“This is a historic first step in the fight to protect youth mental health, and we hope to see this trend continue with similar commitments from other members of the social media industry,” Wyoming Attorney General Keith Kautz said in a press release. 
Wyoming officials are still working to decipher the terms around settlement distribution, Gov. Mark Gordon’s Communication Manager Amy Edmonds said Thursday. Right now it appears likely that the spending won’t be restricted, she said. That means it will probably be funneled into the general fund, which is under the discretion of the Wyoming Legislature. 
“This is a good day for Wyoming’s kids and their parents,” Gordon posted Wednesday on Facebook, noting that he has been working with Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder “to protect Wyoming’s kids from Big Tech’s increasingly sophisticated and pernicious efforts to tantalize them to unfiltered social media.”
For the dozens of states involved, the settlement promises money for mental health programs for kids, including after-school or summer activities and digital literacy counselors. The funding will be allocated in payments over 10 years rather than in lump sums. 
“When it comes to our children, consumer protection is nonnegotiable,” Degenfelder said in a Thursday statement. “I look forward to how these funds can be deployed for online safety and digital literacy initiatives and mental health resources.”
The governor’s office considers the extra guardrails promised in the settlement a huge win, Edmonds said. Kautz echoed that, noting that the safety features “will provide tangible relief to kids in Wyoming, as well as nationwide.”

Colorado Solicitor General Shannon Stevenson, right, hugs a colleague outside of court after tech giant Meta reached a settlement to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction in Oakland, Calif., on Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Noah Berger)

Those features include hard daily time limits with mandatory pauses to interrupt endless scrolling for children; nighttime blocks to restrict access between midnight and 6 a.m.; elimination of push notifications during school hours and improved age-assurance measures. The company has also committed to stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders and content related to suicide and self-harm, as well as new limits on social comparison features.
These represent “groundbreaking” changes to Instagram and Facebook that are “more significant and comprehensive than previously ordered by any court,” the Wyoming AG press release said. “And perhaps most importantly, this settlement represents a down payment toward an industry-wide social media experience that allows kids to connect in a healthy way.”
Consumer protection 
Some 48 states and D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands had claimed the company designed Instagram with addictive features, knowingly exposed young users to serious mental harms and intentionally misled the public about the safety of its platforms, among other things. 
Attorneys general across the country sued Meta individually or as part of a consolidated federal lawsuit. 
Wednesday’s agreement cut short an ongoing court case involving California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, which were among 29 states that sued Meta in 2023. The federal trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, where Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had been among the witnesses expected to take the stand.
Dawson Kelly holds a banner with names of young people who advocates say died as a result of social media outside the Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse on Aug. 18, 2026, in Oakland, Calif. (AP Photo/Noah Berger)
Wednesday’s settlement resolves those cases and claims by the other settling states and territories. It also resolves the states’ claims against Meta for its sharing of nonpublic information about Facebook users with third parties, like Cambridge Analytica, leading up to the 2016 election.
Meta said in a blog post that it is “building on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.”
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the company said in the blog post. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard.”
The company urged competitors TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar safety measures.
The $18 billion settlement is a fraction of Meta’s 2025 revenue of $201 billion. 
Associated Press writer Kelvin Chan reported from London. Kaityn Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writers Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, and Wyatte Grantham-Philips in Chicago contributed to this report.

name: WyoFile
title: Elwood Mead’s hard lessons for a shrinking river
authors: by WyoHistory.org editors Leslie Waggener and Kylie Louise McCormick
description:
A young water engineer came to Wyoming to bring order to the state’s water law. Amid the West’s current drought, his work and legacy are still points of negotiation, write WyoHistory.org editors Leslie Waggener and Kylie McCormick.  
The post Elwood Mead’s hard lessons for a shrinking river appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Elwood Mead arrived in Cheyenne in 1888 to sort out Wyoming’s water law before it had any. Territorial Governor Thomas Moonlight had offered the 30-year-old Mead the job sight unseen. When they finally met, Moonlight had second thoughts: “I had no idea you were so young,” he told Mead. “I’m sure you will fail.”
His name now belongs to Lake Mead, the reservoir behind Hoover Dam, roughly 300 miles downstream from Lake Powell. This summer, both reservoirs hit record lows. The two reservoirs are connected by more than geography. In April, the Bureau of Reclamation held back 1.48 million acre-feet bound for Lake Mead, trading Mead’s levels for Powell’s — buying time before Glen Canyon Dam’s turbines stop generating power entirely. Hoover Dam’s own output, meanwhile, is projected to drop by as much as 40 % this year.
The rules that have governed both reservoirs for nearly two decades are expiring, and the seven river states never reached a deal to replace them. So, on Aug. 21, the federal government stepped in on its own: Lower Basin states must cut back sharply, while Wyoming and the other Upper Basin states face no mandatory reductions — yet. To understand today’s fight over who bears the cuts, it helps to go back to where Elwood Mead’s own story started. 
A system from scratch
Back in Cheyenne, what Mead found was chaos. Territorial settlers, borrowing a mining-camp rule called “prior appropriation” (aka “first in time, first in right”), posted handwritten claims to entire streams, sometimes claiming more than the state really had. “The virtue of self-denial had not been conspicuous” among claimants, Mead later wrote. One judge decided a Cheyenne case by granting water rights unmoored from any ditch or acre of land, then told Mead, who’d asked how to enforce it, to go find each claimant himself.

A young Elwood Mead, circa 1883–1888, during his time teaching at Colorado State Agricultural College — the same fresh-faced engineer who would arrive in Cheyenne soon after to write Wyoming’s water law. (Colorado State University, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Mead’s fix, in the 1890 constitution he helped draft, was blunt: The state would own the water, and a board of control — not a courtroom — would decide disputes, tying rights to water actually used rather than paper claims. Most territorial claims got cut to a fraction of what people thought they owned.
That trade-off paid off most clearly where resistance ran deepest. Buffalo, in Johnson County, had voted against the new constitution and distrusted Cheyenne. In 1891, Mead’s office installed the state’s first stream-gaging station on Clear Creek, the stream that flows through Buffalo that would provide the real test of his system. The adjudication cut most claims on the creek by roughly 90%. A Colorado investment company holding foreclosed Buffalo-area land sued to challenge the results, and the Wyoming Supreme Court upheld the cuts. Then drought hit. Because rights on the creek had already been cut to what it could sustain, every irrigator made it through the season anyway. People who opposed the system became its defenders. A hard technical ceiling, enforced by someone with real authority, had done what open claims and courtroom guesswork could not: survive a crisis.
A man of his era
Mead carried that lesson for the rest of his life. During his years in Washington doing federal irrigation research, he lost his right arm in a 1901 trolley accident after a baseball game, taught himself to write left-handed, and told a friend he expected to “do as well without any hands as with both of them.” He went on to a stint in Australia, then in 1924 took the top job at the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, overseeing construction of Hoover Dam and Boulder City, Nevada, the town built for its workers. He died in 1936, four months after the dam’s dedication; the reservoir was named Lake Mead in his honor within weeks.
Elwood Mead, right, circa 1895 in his Cheyenne office with the Wyoming Nilometer, a device he designed while Wyoming’s territorial engineer. The nilometer was inspired by the ancient Egyptian instruments used to gauge the Nile’s floods, but turned here to measure water applied to irrigated fields. (American Heritage Center, University of Wyoming)
It’s tempting to end there: The young engineer who fixed Wyoming’s water goes on to lead construction of the dam that supplied water to the modern Southwest. But it’s worth understanding Mead on his own terms. He came of age with the Progressive movement’s faith that trained experts could manage natural resources for the public good, the same faith behind national forests and city planning. Mead’s version, “social engineering,” pushed further: government-built farmhouses, planned irrigation colonies, resettlement schemes for struggling families.
Some of it worked, but much of it strained under real-world weight that it wasn’t built to carry. When agricultural prices collapsed during the 1920s farm crisis, residents of one of his model towns in California burned his portrait in the community hall, and Bureau of Reclamation projects he championed left irrigators holding debts they couldn’t repay. Mead was a man of his moment, applying tools past the point where they held.
Same river, different century
Here the story sharpens rather than repeats. Decades of drought have collided with rising demand from the cities and farms the Colorado River supplies. The river has been governed since 1922 by a patchwork of compacts, court decisions and federal law. In February 2026, the Upper Basin states — Wyoming among them — reached consensus; the Lower Basin states rejected it. What’s stuck is two blocs, evenly matched.
The disagreement comes down to whose water absorbs the pain. Lower Basin states, which draw from the river’s two largest reservoirs, want Upper Basin states to accept mandatory cuts, too. Upper Basin officials counter that they already cut back in dry years by necessity because they lack big reservoirs on that same scale. They’re not wrong: The river’s average flow has dropped by roughly 20% since 2000.
Wyoming’s negotiator holds Mead’s old job. State Engineer Brandon Gebhart has warned that leaning on Flaming Gorge Reservoir — fed by the Green River, Wyoming’s own contribution to the Colorado — as a permanent relief valve is a finite tool, not a solution. Lower Basin negotiators see it differently: Tto them, Upper Basin reservoirs are exactly the flexibility a shrinking river needs. Gebhart has pushed for continued negotiation to avoid litigation.
One federal lever resembles what Mead built: the agency deciding which states gets cuts is the Bureau of Reclamation, the same one Mead once ran. Some would call that the kind of impartial authority that Mead spent his career building. Others would call it federal overreach into water that seven states consider their own, an irony given that Mead himself resisted federal involvement in reclamation for years before reluctantly coming around. Whether the authority holds, and whether it should, is very much unresolved. On Aug. 24, Nevada sued to find out, asking a court to block the Bureau of Reclamation’s plan.
Crises are often what push societies to change what they’d otherwise leave alone. Mead built his career on that premise. He turned Wyoming’s crisis into permanent law, then spent the rest of his life trying to scale that same fix to bigger problems, not all of which held. Whether the Colorado River Basin can do what Mead did, at the scale this crisis now demands, is the open question behind every headline about Lake Mead’s shrinking shoreline.

name: WyoFile
title: Mountain frames highlight abundant stars
description:
On a recent summer adventure, WyoFile's Daniel Kenah caught fish and captured stars.
The post Mountain frames highlight abundant stars appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
What is a Wyoming summer without adventure? Last week, three friends and I trekked into the backcountry to experience some of the best the Equality State has to offer.
Loon Lake, just outside Yellowstone National Park, gives an exceptional remove from summer crowds and light pollution, allowing for some fun night photography. The namesake loons’ melancholy call — extremely rare in Wyoming — provided a beautiful punctuation to the thick silence.
After two days coaxing Yellowstone cutthroat trout from their hiding holes, we struck off to new waters — and much older mountains — in the Absaroka Range.
The Wiggins Fork of the Wind River drops almost due south from the Absarokas to Dubois; the wide drainage framed the night sky, drawing my eye to the North Star. 






Click to enlarge: The distant glow of Cody brightens the horizon in this one-hour exposure from the Wiggins Fork on Aug. 22, 2026. (Daniel Kenah/WyoFile)






In this 30-minute exposure, the Milky Way can be seen from the Wiggins Fork on Aug. 22, 2026. (Daniel Kenah/WyoFile)


Despite the glow from Cody, roughly 50 miles north-northeast, the dark sky gives a rare view of our Milky Way.
Wyoming, where dark skies abound, is a great place to look up.

title: Following years of turmoil, county approves contract with Pueblo sheriff union
description: Pueblo County commissioners Thursday approved a collective bargaining agreement for the county sheriff’s office more than two years after its employees first voted to form a union.  The agreement follows years of turmoil between union leadership and outgoing Pueblo Sheriff David Lucero, a Democrat, who claimed in a lawsuit that a Colorado law that allows […]
text:
Leaders with different unions around Pueblo held a silent protest during the Pueblo County Commissioners meeting on Feb. 25, 2025, outside of the Pueblo County Government Building. (Photo courtesy of Brad Riccillo)Pueblo County commissioners Thursday approved a collective bargaining agreement for the county sheriff’s office more than two years after its employees first voted to form a union. 
The agreement follows years of turmoil between union leadership and outgoing Pueblo Sheriff David Lucero, a Democrat, who claimed in a lawsuit that a Colorado law that allows collective bargaining of county employees does not apply to sheriff offices. 
Lucero’s lawsuit, filed in December 2024, argued a county sheriff is not included under Colorado’s statutory definition of a county, as sheriff is its own elected constitutional office, and the law does not apply to his agency. A judge dismissed part of the lawsuit in July, and attorneys for the state asked the judge to dismiss the remaining claims earlier in August. Lucero told commissioners Thursday that he intends to direct legal counsel to pull the remaining claims. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The agreement sufficiently addresses the concerns that led me to seek judicial review, and I do not believe continued litigation is necessary or in the best interests of Pueblo County,” Lucero said. “I also believe ending the litigation is the fiscally responsible decision. There is no reason to continue spending taxpayer dollars litigating issues that we’ve been able to resolve through negotiation.”
County commissioners previously approved at least $45,000 to fund legal counsel for Lucero in the lawsuit.  
Lucero lost the Democratic primary in his reelection bid in June to Allen Medina. Leroy Mora, an unaffiliated candidate, is also running for sheriff in the November election. Medina and Mora have both expressed support for the sheriff’s union. 



Quotation







The sheriff's office has been in existence for over 160 years, and there's never been a formal bargaining unit that is able to speak on the employees' behalf and have it actually be a written promise between both sides that we will work together, we will work harmoniously.


– Brad Riccillo, president of the International Brotherhood of Police Officers Local 837


Brad Riccillo, an employee of the sheriff’s office and president of the International Brotherhood of Police Officers Local 837, the state-recognized union for Pueblo Sheriff’s Office employees, said the agreement is essentially a “boilerplate contract” to create a fair starting point for the union to work with. He said he’s proud of the work those supporting the union put in to get to this point. 
“The sheriff’s office has been in existence for over 160 years, and there’s never been a formal bargaining unit that is able to speak on the employees’ behalf and have it actually be a written promise between both sides that we will work together, we will work harmoniously,” Riccillo said. 
The union brought in a federal mediator to get through the last round of bargaining, Riccillo said. He’s particularly happy that the agreement includes quarterly meetings between sheriff’s office leadership and union leadership to talk about any issues that arise between contract negotiations, he said. 
More than half of the employees in the sheriff’s office, 220, are union members, according to Riccillo.
Reassigned to clerical work
Peter Blood, who works with the Pueblo County attorney’s office, said the contract is an “excellent beginning, but nowhere near where we need to be in the future in terms of our relationship with the labor world.” 
At the Thursday meeting, Riccillo thanked the commissioners, local labor advocates, the national IBPO team and former state Rep. Daneya Esgar, a Pueblo Democrat who sponsored the bill allowing county employees to unionize. 
“The journey was never easy,” Riccillo said. “We faced skepticism, legal and administrative hurdles, a lawsuit, retaliation, demotions, terminations and difficult days that tested our resolve. Yet through every obstacle, our members never wavered, and our numbers never dropped.”
Lucero told commissioners his main responsibility has always been to protect his staff, taxpayers of Pueblo County and the statutory responsibilities of his office. 
“When questions arose about how Colorado’s new collective bargaining law intersected with those responsibilities, I believe those were legitimate legal questions that needed clarification,” Lucero said. “At the same time, once directed to bargain, we did so, and we continued negotiating while those legal questions were being addressed.”
The union in 2024 filed an unfair labor practice complaint with the state over Lucero’s refusal to engage in collective bargaining. The Colorado Department of Labor and Employment denied Lucero’s appeal of the state decisions saying he must bargain with the union before filing the lawsuit, and Lucero then filed the lawsuit against the state and the union. 
The department dismissed a different unfair labor practice complaint the union filed related to wages in May. 
In 2024, Lucero reassigned Riccillo to clerical work in a move that labor advocates claimed was retaliation for working with the union. 
Riccillo is still working in a clerical role. He said he’ll speak to the next sheriff about his options after the November election determines who will succeed Lucero.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho US Rep. Simpson hopes to increase resources for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis
description: Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson this year is looking to boost federal funding for tribes to address the ongoing Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis. Simpson chairs the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee. The subcommittee in June advanced a budget with a 26% increase to the Bureau[...]
text:
A panel of women testifying on Nov. 20, 2024, to the House Appropriations Committee oversight hearing, chaired by Idaho U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, on Investigating the Crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women listen as Maulian Bryant (left) spoke about the challenges her Penobscot Nation faces in accessing resources to find missing people. From left to right: Mary Jane Miles, Cheryl Horn, Abigail Echo-Hawk and Eugenia Charles-Newton. (Screenshot via YouTube/House Appropriations Committee)Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson this year is looking to boost federal funding for tribes to address the ongoing Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis.
Chairman of the Interior, Environment and Related Agencies subcommittee U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, looks on during a House Appropriations Committee hearing at the Rayburn House Office Building on April 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
Simpson chairs the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee. The subcommittee in June advanced a budget with a 26% increase to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, which includes:

an additional $142 million for criminal investigations and police services
$17 million for law enforcement special initiatives 
$33 million specifically for missing and murdered Indigenous women, which is about a $14.5 million increase over the fiscal year 2026 appropriation. 
$5 million for the use of forensic genealogy to identify missing and murdered individuals in unsolved cases through the bureau’s Operation Spirit Return.  

“We put a bunch more money into tribal justice, and that’s hard in a year when we’re trying to reduce spending at the federal level,” Simpson said in an interview. 
As a result, he said other portions of the budget, such as funding for the Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service and the Smithsonian Institution all saw reductions. 
“But I’ve said from the beginning: We’re not going to try to balance the budget on the back of the tribes,” Simpson said. “These are trust and treaty responsibilities we’ve got with our Native American brothers and sisters, and we’ve got to keep those. ” 
Coeur d’Alene Tribe Chairman Chief J. Allan told the Idaho Capital Sun in an emailed statement that the tribe supports the effort.
“The issue has gotten more attention in recent years, and Congressman Simpson recognizes that serious problems require adequate funding,” Allan said. “While the focus on MMIP is critical, he also recognizes that the tragic situation is the direct result of decades of public safety and justice deficiencies across Indian Country.  Addressing those shortfalls across the system will help improve conditions overall, as well as prevent missing and murdered incidents in the future.” 
Marco Ovando, spokesman for the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes, said there was still a lot of work to be done to address the MMIP crisis.
“The crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous People within Idaho and the United States is still largely being unaddressed despite national attention in recent years,” Ovando wrote in an emailed statement from the Tribes. “While the Idaho Legislature has created a taskforce in 2020 and a report 2021, state-tribal collaboration remains very limited. … We have a case as recent as this spring where the investigation has produced very little resulting in families without closure, frustrated leadership, and a community left on edge. We hope Congress will appropriate more funding to address these shortfalls because our people are tired of the pain and sorrow and lack of help.”
Leaders from the Nez Perce, Shoshone-Bannock, and Kootenai Tribes could not be reached for comment. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What is the scope of the MMIP crisis in Idaho? 

A 2021 Boise State University report found that 75% of missing Indigenous people in Idaho were women, and the average missing persons rate was higher for Indigenous persons in Idaho. 
Boise State report: 75% of missing Indigenous people in Idaho are women

Idaho’s average missing persons rate was approximately 10.59 per 100,000 persons. The average rate for Indigenous persons in Idaho rose to 18.99 per 100,000 persons, according to the report.
Boise State completed the study at the direction of the Idaho Legislature, which passed House Concurrent Resolution 33 in 2020 and declared the issue of missing and murdered Indigenous women a crisis. 
There were 79 missing Native Americans in Idaho reported in the 2023 Idaho Missing Persons Clearinghouse. 
Nationwide, Indigenous women are murdered at 10 times the national average, according to the National Indigenous Women’s Resource Center. 
Simpson said as a Blackfoot native growing up along the border of the Fort Hall Reservation, he thought he understood issues affecting Native American tribes. 
“And I realized I didn’t when I got on the Interior Appropriations Committee,” Simpson said. 
He said a couple years ago, he saw an Idaho Public Television show in which an advocate cited national statistics that approximately 6,000 Indigenous people are murdered or go missing each year. 
“I’m sitting there going, ‘That’s twice as many people as we lost on 9/11, and yet I’ve never heard this.’ And being as close as I was with Indian issues over the years, I’m kind of shocked that I’d never heard this,” Simpson said. 
 Jurisdictional, other changes may be needed to solve issue 

Simpson, both in the interview with the Sun and at a July hearing held by the House Committee on Natural Resources regarding the MMIP crisis, highlighted issues with jurisdiction.
He said sometimes it can be unclear if Tribal police, local city or county law enforcement or the FBI has jurisdiction in cases, especially those that cross out of reservation boundaries. And these entities often don’t have formal agreements to work with each other. This uncertainty can lengthen the response time. 
“Tribal police officers go through the same training as our county police officers do, our state police officers do. Their judges go through the same training as our judges do, and so forth. They’re every bit as competent to do the job as anybody else is, and we ought to let them do their job more,” Simpson said. “But there are still places where counties that are adjacent to reservations don’t have memorandums of understanding.” 
Ovando, of the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes, said cross-jurisdictional barriers as well as limited funding are “are hampering efforts to create a more successful and comprehensive plan in adequately addressing the crisis.”
“Being a rural tribe on the Idaho-Nevada Stateline has also limited approach due to geography,” he said. “Simply gaining resources like law enforcement are a challenge. ”
Leaders from the Nez Perce Tribe also told Idaho Reports in 2023 that jurisdiction was an issue, including a lack of access to other law enforcement data systems. Data can also be an issue if a Tribal citizen is found dead outside of a reservation and their race is misidentified. 
Nez Perce Chief Judge Natasha Anderson also noted to Idaho Reports that Idaho’s definition of peace officer doesn’t include tribal officers who attend the Indian Police Academy, rather than the state’s Peace Officer Standards Training Academy, called POST. Otherwise, the officers must be deputized by a county sheriff or city chief of police, which often doesn’t occur because of Tribal sovereignty, then-Nez Perce Tribe’s Interim Police Chief Leotis McCormack said at the time.
At the July hearing, Simpson questioned Charles Addington, principal director in the Office of Justice Services of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, about jurisdictional issues. Addington said the bureau was working on cross-deputization and trying to close jurisdictional gaps. 
“This should not be this damn complicated,” Simpson said at the hearing, “and somehow we’ve got to change that.”
