name: Colorado Newsline
title: At their 1876 convention, Colorado Democrats hoped for an upset in the first state elections
description: One week after Republicans met in Pueblo, Colorado Democrats convened their first state convention at Manitou Springs on Aug. 29, 1876. A special train from Denver, ferrying as many as 200 convention-bound passengers, “was handsomely decorated with flags and banners bearing the name of (Democratic presidential and vice-presidential candidates Samuel) Tilden[...]
text:
The town of Manitou Springs is pictured in this photograph dated between 1881 and 1883. Colorado Democrats held their first-ever state political convention there in 1876. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-1527)
One week after Republicans met in Pueblo, Colorado Democrats convened their first state convention at Manitou Springs on Aug. 29, 1876.



← Aug. 20–26
Aug. 27–Sept. 2 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

A special train from Denver, ferrying as many as 200 convention-bound passengers, “was handsomely decorated with flags and banners bearing the name of (Democratic presidential and vice-presidential candidates Samuel) Tilden and (Thomas) Hendricks,” reported the Colorado Springs Gazette. “All the vehicles in this place and Manitou were pressed into service to convey the delegates and others to the Springs.”
One nomination to be made by the convention was never in doubt. Thomas Patterson, an Irish-American Denver lawyer, had become the first Democrat ever elected to higher office in Colorado in 1874, when voters elected him as the Territory’s non-voting delegate to Congress.
The “Little Democratic Tiger,” as the Gazette called him, represented the party’s best hope in a state that was otherwise expected to lean Republican. Patterson opened the convention with a speech made to “deafening cheers,” and he was unanimously acclaimed as the Democratic nominee to return to Congress, this time as the state’s at-large representative.
In the Centennial State’s first election, scheduled for the first Tuesday in October, Coloradans would in fact vote for the office twice — first to fill out the remainder of a term in the 44th Congress, and separately for a full term to begin in 1877.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Though William A.H. Loveland, a prominent railroad investor from the Democratic stronghold of Golden, was tipped as a possible favorite to win the party’s nomination for governor, in the end it was Denver businessman Bela M. Hughes who got the nod. Like the GOP, the Democrats offered the lieutenant governor post as a concession of sorts to delegates from southern Colorado, nominating Michael Beshoar, a physician and prominent citizen of Las Animas County, as Hughes’ running mate.
The Golden Transcript, a Democratic newspaper, applauded the convention’s nomination of a slate “well calculated to satisfy all portions of the state and all elements in the party,” and predicted that with Hughes “so well and favorably known to every citizen of the state,” Democrats could hope to pull off a major political upset in October.
But most other Colorado papers leaned Republican, and their published accounts of the Democratic convention made no attempt to hide their partisan loyalties. Rocky Mountain News publisher William Byers had been a GOP delegate in Pueblo, and his paper denounced speeches by Democrats for their “extreme partisan bitterness” and “vituperation and personal abuse of Republican leaders.”
“The speaker would undoubtedly have hissed it through his set teeth if had not been so unfortunately deficient in those members,” wrote the News’ correspondent of one delegate. “As it was he breathed out threatenings and slaughter and railing accusation very much as if his mouth had been full of hot mush.”
The News, however, wasn’t entirely incapable of printing kind words about its political opponents, praising the Democratic convention’s “most admirable secretary — Mr. Alva Adams, of Del Norte.”
“Alva is so clever that he is sometimes taken for a Republican,” the correspondent wrote. “He is a candidate for the legislature, and if it is necessary to have a Democrat in that body, he is my choice.”
The 26-year-old Adams would, in fact, be elected to the first General Assembly, and eventually served three nonconsecutive terms as Colorado governor. Both his brother and son would follow him in high office, making 1876 the start of a political dynasty that would last until World War II.



Selected sources

The Colorado Springs Gazette, Sept. 2, 1876
The Rocky Mountain News, Sept. 1, 1876
The Golden Transcript, Sept. 6, 1876

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee hunting, fishing license fees could increase 29% next year to help fill budget deficit
description: Tennessee hunting and fishing license fees could increase by an average of 29% next year in an effort to bridge a multi-million-dollar deficit in the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency’s budget.  The Tennessee Fish and Wildlife Commission, TWRA’s governing body, approved new license fees along with the agency’s 2027-2028 budget on Aug. 21.  The new fee […]
text:
The Tennessee Fish and Wildlife Commission, TWRA’s governing body, approved new license fees along with the agency’s 2027-2028 budget on Aug. 21, 2026. The increased fees must still be approved by the Tennessee General Assembly. (Photo: John Partipilo, Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee hunting and fishing license fees could increase by an average of 29% next year in an effort to bridge a multi-million-dollar deficit in the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency’s budget. 
The Tennessee Fish and Wildlife Commission, TWRA’s governing body, approved new license fees along with the agency’s 2027-2028 budget on Aug. 21. 
The new fee structure will now go before the Tennessee General Assembly’s Joint Government Operations Committee, likely in December, according to TWRA Business Operations Deputy Director Frank Fiss. If the fee structure passes through that committee, the earliest it could take effect is July 1, 2027. 
“We don’t like to have to raise the fees, but we have to consider it at this time. Our costs … have gone up at least 40% since the last license increase in 2015,” Fiss said. “The dollar we had in 2015 has the buying power of 71 cents today, and we have struggled to keep our services at the level they’re at.”
Lawmakers look for long-term fix to Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency’s budget woes

All together, the license adjustments total a 29% increase in revenue, equivalent to about $12 million. The structure of some licenses may also look different. For example, big game hunters could pay license fees based on the game they hunt (deer, turkey, elk or bear, for instance) rather than the current fee structure that is based on hunting method (gun, archery or muzzleloader).
“Some license experiences for customers may go down a little. Some may be very similar (to current fees), some may go up more than 29%,” Fiss said. “When you look at it en masse, it’s a 29% increase.”
Annual hunting and fishing combination licenses would go from $33 to $42. The senior rate for the annual combination license would increase from $4 to $21. 
The fee for an annual all-inclusive sportsman license would increase from $165 to $185. Youth sportsman licenses would increase from $9 to $12, and senior sportsman licenses would nearly double in cost from $49 to $95.
The license fee changes come after failed attempts to secure dedicated state funding for the agency’s Wildlife Fund, which is used to maintain wildlife management areas, fish stocking, enforcement and shooting ranges. TWRA Executive Director Jason Maxedon said the agency’s budget has been strained as the state legislature has placed more responsibility on TWRA but not provided additional funding sources to cover extra costs. 
License fees make up 38% of the agency’s annual funding for fish and wildlife projects. Federal taxes on hunting and fishing equipment and a state tax on real estate transfers also contribute.
The Tennessee Fish and Wildlife Commission previously approved license fee increases in 2024, but withdrew the changes after opposition from the General Assembly.
“That opposition came with assurances of support for dedicated funding,” Maxedon said. “We appreciate the lawmakers who carried that legislation for us, but when it failed to pass this session, it sent us back to our original proposal.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama to borrow $200 million to build new Escambia prison
description: A state board Thursday agreed to borrow almost $200 million to build a new 4,000 bed prison in Escambia County. The decision by the Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority increases the budget for the Escambia construction project from $700 million to $900 million, on top of more than $1.25 billion spent to build another 4,000 […]
text:
Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, speaks with media following the Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority meeting on Thursday, August 27, 2026. The committee approved borrowing up to $195 million to pay for the construction of a new men’s prison in Escambia County. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)A state board Thursday agreed to borrow almost $200 million to build a new 4,000 bed prison in Escambia County.
The decision by the Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority increases the budget for the Escambia construction project from $700 million to $900 million, on top of more than $1.25 billion spent to build another 4,000 bed prison in Elmore County.
Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, a member of the authority and the outgoing chair of the Senate Finance and Taxation General Fund Committee, said the borrowing for the prison in Atmore was “a long time in coming, but we got it done.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The principal thing we are doing is we are starting the Atmore facility,” he said. “This allows us to actually move forward with the Escambia facility.”
The Alabama Legislature in 2021 approved a total of $1.3 billion to build the two prisons, which supporters said would be safer for inmates and correctional officers and allow the Alabama Department of Corrections to shut down older facilities, saving the department money.
However, the process has been rocky. The Elmore County prison, named the Gov. Kay Ivey Correctional Complex, has consumed nearly all of the money originally appropriated for the project, and lawmakers have not committed to shutting down any existing prison.
Corrections declined comment on Thursday. ACIFA also approved a resolution regarding the design, construction management and other services, as well as to advertise bids for the construction of the Escambia prison.
A third resolution approved the transfer of the Ivey complex from ADOC to ACIFA. The prison is scheduled to be completed in October.
“There is a small portion of land on which we have facilities where there is a question as to ownership or rights, so we are correcting that,” Albritton said.
The resolution allows investors to place a bid on bonds for a maximum total of $195 million. Investors will bid on the amount they want to invest and the interest rate they expect to earn to provide the money needed for the construction project.
Albritton said the first step is securing investors for the bonds and receiving bids from contractors for construction. He anticipates the project will take 30 months to complete once construction begins on the site anticipated for October.
Albritton expects the Escambia prison to cost less than roughly $1.3 billion to build the Elmore facility.
“The Alabama Legislature, working with the Governor’s Office and ADOC and others, were able to search the sofa cushions to pull forth from areas that we needed to for a number of years,” he said. “There was some intentional penny-pinching along the way, and that is why we are where we are.”
The new prison construction will replace beds and not add capacity, according to the handout provided by ADOC. The Escambia prison is planned to be built in two parts. The first part of the project will be 195 acres on property located next to Fountain Correctional Facility near Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore. It will comprise more than 2,000 beds and 26 buildings.
“Ultimately Fountain will be demolished and removed from service in connection with the construction and opening of the new Escambia County facility,” according to a media sheet provided by ADOC at the meeting.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Outgoing lawmaker fears private-school vouchers will haunt Tennessee
description: State Rep. Caleb Hemmer is leaving the Tennessee Legislature with the feeling he made a mark in just two terms but with major concern that lawmakers passed private-school voucher programs that will prove too costly for the state to stomach. While some Democrats aren’t allowed to pass any bills, Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat, passed a […]
text:
Rep. Caleb Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat retiring after two terms in office, calls the legislature's move to create private school vouchers "the single worst policy decision" of his time in office. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)State Rep. Caleb Hemmer is leaving the Tennessee Legislature with the feeling he made a mark in just two terms but with major concern that lawmakers passed private-school voucher programs that will prove too costly for the state to stomach.
While some Democrats aren’t allowed to pass any bills, Hemmer, a Nashville Democrat, passed a children’s mental health bill and another measure this year designating Nashville hot chicken as an official state food, while working on policy and budgeting behind the scenes and focusing on constituent needs. 
Yet his gun-storage bill designed to cut down on thefts went nowhere, as did a provision that would have shone a light on the state’s newest private-school voucher and put income limits on the program. 
Hemmer doesn’t think Republicans who enacted the state’s two private-school voucher programs have completely given up on public schools. But he considers it “very shortsighted and misguided policy.” 
Beyond that, he said, lawmakers who voted for the state’s two private-school programs are “more scared of the voucher lobby and Jeff Yass of Pennsylvania,” referring to the billionaire who pours money into political action committees — including Club For Growth — that focus solely on vouchers than worried about solid education policy.
“You either get in line or you pay for the crime, and they’ll spend millions of dollars against you,” he said. “I think it’ll go down as the single worst public policy decision we made during my term for sure. It’s not gonna improve outcomes. It’s not gonna make public schools better by any means. It just costs more money for the taxpayers.”
Tennessee won’t know how many new vouchers go to existing private school students

Besides giving out money, mainly to students who were enrolled already in private schools, the state requires few “accountability measures,” Hemmer pointed out. The legislature this year stripped any requirement that students receiving the “scholarship” vouchers take the state’s main achievement test, only a national test, meaning Tennessee has no way to compare students’ performance.
Gov. Bill Lee, who made them his main initiative over eight years, went “all-in” for vouchers “for better or worse,” Hemmer said. “I just fear it’s going to be for the worse. Think of all the things we can do in education policy that evidence has backed.”
Republican gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, likely the next governor, is backing school “choice,” though she has shied away from saying she would expand it beyond the legally allowed number of 5,000 students annually. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jerri Green, a Memphis City Council member, is pledging to defund vouchers if elected.
In the backdrop
Indianapolis-based EdChoice Legal Advocates, a school “choice” group, has filed a motion to end an ACLU-backed challenge to the state’s newest private-school voucher program. 
A hearing is coming up in Davidson County Chancery Court where Jefferson County parent Denise Fair and her husband, both first responders, are seeking to intervene. They worked extra jobs to pay the tuition for their two youngest daughters to attend private schools, and the state funds have cut the burden.
“It has allowed me more time to dedicate to attending activities with the girls and freed up enough financial resources to allow the girls to attend some school field trips,” Denise Fair said in a statement.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
EdChoice is also representing Mike and Monica Sweeney of Knoxville, who rely on the money to send their children to a Catholic school after pulling them out of another school and homeschooling because of concerns about COVID-19 guidelines, according to a statement.
Their action comes in response to litigation by a group of 10 Tennessee parents and taxpayers who filed suit in November 2025 challenging the constitutionality of the state’s “universal” private-school voucher program, claiming it shifts funds to unaccountable private schools that “openly discriminate” against students.
In its first year, the program provided vouchers worth $7,300 to 20,000 students at a cost of $144 million, plus all the extras to entice passage. Lawmakers initially approved money for 10,000 students whose family incomes hit 300% of the federal subsidized lunch program, about $180,000, and 10,000 for students with no family income requirement.
Before even seeing how well it worked, lawmakers expanded the program this year to 35,000 students, pushing the cost above $260 million and the state’s total expense for private-school vouchers, including an initial program for low-income kids passed in 2019, well past the $300 million mark.
The fight might never end.
Senate Democrats pounced on the latest figures showing public school students receive less in state funding than private-school voucher students.
Their numbers show Lee and Republican lawmakers put $6.9 billion toward K-12 schools for this school year, $7,272 per student, about $260 less on average than those in the private-school voucher program receive, $7,530. Students in the Education Savings Account program receive even more from the state, roughly $9,000, even as their performance appears to be flagging.
Lawmakers took federal money under the Obama administration for the Race to the Top program, which some critics have referred to as the “Race Over the Edge,” turning an end-of-year test into the end-all-be-all of education.
Many teachers believe the move took the joy out of teaching, forcing them to “teach to the test” instead of focusing on fundamentals and expanding the mind (not through psychedelia). 
That view goes out the door, though, now that the state is pouring money into private schools.
And while lawmakers such as Hemmer want a better accounting of the number of private-school students who received the money, Lee made no secret he was writing a check for private-school kids and parents when they surrounded him during the Capitol bill-signing ceremony two years ago.
Even some of the state’s staunchest Republicans call it a “give-away.” But by the time the state hits a financial crisis because of this government expansion, it might be too late to turn back.
More historical accuracy, please
Page four of ” Marsha Blackburn Coloring Book An American Story,” depicts an idyllic version of life in the South. (Tennessee Lookout copy)
A new coloring book surfaced recently in support of Blackburn’s gubernatorial bid, displaying her in the idyllic setting of a Mississippi upbringing and, we might add, looking about 30 years younger. We’re told it wasn’t sanctioned by her campaign.
While it shows her wrapped in swaddling clothes, picnicking with the fam, going to school, helping others and visiting the local community theater, the coloring book leaves out a few minor details. It shows no “colored only” water fountains or segregated schools and theaters, nor does it mention the murders of three voter rights activists by the KKK in Neshoba County, Mississippi, which took place about the time Blackburn would have been 12 years old.
In short, while it mentions “Southern roots, strong values, and bright future,” the book glosses over the harsh reality of living in Mississippi and much of the South for Black Americans in the 1960s and ’70s. Then again, it is only a book that requires people to keep their colors within the lines.
Winning friends
Republican U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger introduced a federal bill Thursday that would have gone over well with Mayberry’s Morrison sisters, who used a “flower-making machine” to create their medicinal “elixir” on “The Andy Griffith Show.” (Admission: I had to look up their name.)
Steve Earle wants a word: Earle, center, singer and songwriter of “Copperhead Road,” a ditty about raising weed in East Tennessee, may approve of U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbargers’s move to legalize moonshining. Earle is pictured with House Speaker Cameron Sexton and Rep. Bo Mitchell. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Harshbarger is sponsoring the Freedom to Home Distill Act, which would do exactly what it says, end the prohibition on distilling spirits at home and provide the tax-free, personal-use exemption enjoyed by beer and wine brewers.
“Distilling has deep roots in Tennessee and across Appalachia, tied to self-reliance and craftsmanship that go back generations. It’s long past time we modernize this outdated federal law,” said Harshbarger, who hails from Kingsport.
“Moonshiners” TV series star Eric “Digger” Manes brought the idea to her, saying even the nation’s first president, George Washington, made moonshine.
“Given that multiple states have legalized marijuana, it appears logical that we should be permitted to engage in our hobby without facing repercussions,” Manes said in a statement.
Apparently, he didn’t run that statement by Tennessee’s top GOP lawmakers. But it’s a start. 
Of course, without the prohibition we wouldn’t have some of the state’s most popular tunes, one of which was sung on the state House floor.
“You hardly ever saw Grandaddy down here / He only come to town about twice a year / He’d buy a hundred pounds of yeast and some copper line / Everybody knew that he made moonshine.”*
*”Copperhead Road,” Steve Earle

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Coal, gas naming rights deals don’t erase outsized rate hikes, extractive harm done to WV
description: In September 2025, for the first time in its 55-year-old history, West Virginia University announced it had sold naming rights for the former WVU Coliseum to energy company, Hope Gas. Under a 10-year agreement, it will be known as “Hope Coliseum.” According to the university, the deal covers sponsorships and future donations to athletics.
text:
West Virginia University announced last year that it had sold naming rights for the former WVU Coliseum to energy company, Hope Gas. Under a 10-year agreement, it will be known as “Hope Coliseum.” (Photo courtesy of Hope Gas) In September 2025, for the first time in its 55-year-old history, West Virginia University announced it had sold naming rights for the former WVU Coliseum to energy company, Hope Gas. Under a 10-year agreement, it will be known as “Hope Coliseum.” According to the university, the deal covers sponsorships and future donations to athletics. 
With that, Hope Gas executed a tried and true soft power move. Coal and gas display a masterclass in marketing masked as community care. 
Here’s the playbook: imbed with our flagship university and football, our two holy grails. Yes, it helps our community, but also, this should be the bare minimum. It’s sneaky. There’s an ulterior motive. In this way, gas makes passive income while amassing social currency. Meanwhile, football players and students do the heavy lifting. What a sweet deal. The name Hope Gas is now repeated at every football game. They bought power by association. Doors open when you have that much money. 
But the spin started earlier with the name “Hope.” It’s doublespeak. There is nothing hopeful about thousands of orphaned oil wells oozing methane across West Virginia to the smell of sulfur and rotting eggs. Constant rate hikes are not hopeful. 
West Virginia is no stranger to rhetoric. Friends of Coal wrote the game decades earlier. The PR campaign, masterfully scripted by Charles Ryan Associates, was the most efficacious propaganda drive in our state’s history. 
Friends of Coal is free to join. It cemented likability in a time of decreased coal revenue, black lung spikes and environment spoilage. The once ubiquitous Friends of Coal bumper sticker built political favoritism. It created social capital. But it wasn’t alone. It stands alongside euphemistic names like American Water, Patriot Coal, Mountaineer Gas, Freedom Energy, Liberty Energy and slogans like “Coal Keeps the Lights On.” 
And it’s very strategic that extractive industries financially support sports. Here’s the truth: Football doesn’t make people think about pollution; it makes people cheer. If we can say the name of a company and WVU in the same sentence, our brains scramble. We start associating coal with knowledge. But hear me out: A sweet naming rights deal is not a substitute for accountability. 
The Friends of Coal campaign oval sticker with a black swoop — like a sideways smile — should be studied as the most effective social marketing coup in West Virginia history. 
The “I Love Mountains” sticker — with a heart representing the word love — created by long-time activist and former West Virginia Highland Conservancy member Julian Martin, tried to counter it. He spread awareness about mountaintop removal mining. It was effective. 
But coal had money. They had sponsorships. The “Friends of Coal Bowl” was a PR branding strategy from 2006-2012 where WVU thrashed poor Marshall in football each year. 
The cost of this campaign was pocket change compared to billions coal companies syphoned off. Not to mention billions in subsidies and mine damage. A logo doesn’t restore a stream. It does not heal lungs choking on coal dust. It does not build back a mountain. 
And gas? It became the new coal. The Ohio River Valley Institute, reported an estimated 50,000 abandoned oil and gas wells in the Mountain State needing to be plugged. Many more are unrecorded. It’s corporate negligence. And that number continues rising. As it does, the number of inspectors drops. It’s shameful. 
Here’s the thing: It costs as much as $100,000 dollars to plug a well. What company would ever want to when they can get away with the public holding the bag? It’s like the old saying: socialized loss and privatized profit. Meanwhile, gas bills spike.
You see, we need responsibility. We need accountability. Who pays for cleanup? Who assumes the risk? A corporate sponsorship doesn’t erase that question. 
Hope Gas increases profit. Rates spike. In 2024, Hope Gas requested an astonishing 40% rate hike. In 2025, they reduced their initial ask to 21%. (Notice how they increase it as high as they can get away with?) It’s unconscionable. 
Hope Gas has asked for another rate increase. Rest assured, there will be more. Regulators have scheduled a hearing on the request for September 23rd in Charleston.
Is this despair or hope? The public can decide. Meanwhile, a coliseum screams Hope; and the crowd cheers.

title: Second Alabama medical cannabis store set to open in Talledega
description: Alabama’s second medical cannabis dispensary is set to open Friday in Talladega about three months after the first storefront opened in Montgomery. The dispensary will be the second location of Callie’s Apothecary, the first medical cannabis dispensary to open in the state. When the program is fully up and running, there will be 12 dispensaries […]
text:
Mock medical cannabis gummies in a display case at Callie's Apothecary in Montgomery, Alabama, on May 14, 2026. A second Callie's Apothecary location is set to open in Talledega on Friday, which will be the second dispensary in the state. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s second medical cannabis dispensary is set to open Friday in Talladega about three months after the first storefront opened in Montgomery.
The dispensary will be the second location of Callie’s Apothecary, the first medical cannabis dispensary to open in the state. When the program is fully up and running, there will be 12 dispensaries across the state between four companies. 
“The opening of medical cannabis dispensaries is a milestone for Alabama’s medical cannabis program,” said Sam Blakemore, chair of the Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission (AMCC), in a statement. “Having more dispensary locations throughout the state is vital for patient access and affordability.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Vince Schilleci, owner of Callie’s Apothecary, said in a phone interview Thursday that the Talledega location will ease the travel burden for patients in the northern half of the state until more dispensaries open.
“Hopefully it’ll help patients that have been on the fence of whether or not they wanted to try this, but didn’t want to drive to Montgomery. Perhaps it’s a little bit closer for them now,” he said. “We’re just happy to now have multiple locations in the state to make it a little bit easier for those patients that are having to travel.” 
The Montgomery location opened in June, five years after the Legislature approved a medical cannabis program and after several rounds of litigation over the state program, particularly in the granting of licenses. 
The store reported doing about $15,000 worth of sales in its first week of operation. According to the release, over 800 patients have made more than 1,300 transactions at the Montgomery location. 
Three of the companies, CCS of Alabama, LLC, GP6 Wellness, LLC, and RJK Holdings, LLC, have licenses. A fourth license is pending litigation, but is likely to go to Yellowhammer Medical Dispensaries, LLC.
According to the statement, GP6 Wellness expects to open BamaBloom dispensaries in Athens and Birmingham in September. A third location is planned for Etowah County. CCS of Alabama expects to open its third Callie’s Apothecary location in Bessemer in September. 
RJK Holdings has locations planned in Oxford, Mobile, and Daphne, according to the statement.
The Alabama medical cannabis law, enacted in 2021, allows registered physicians to recommend cannabis for about 15 medical conditions, including cancer, depression, Parkinson’s Disease, PTSD, sickle-cell anemia, chronic pain, and terminal diseases. 
People who suffer from the qualifying conditions must get approval from their physician and enter the patient registry in order to buy products at a dispensary.
The approved product forms are restricted to tablets, tinctures, patches, oils, and gel cubes (only peach flavor), with raw plant material and smokable forms remaining prohibited.
“Alabama law tightly regulates businesses in the medical cannabis industry and rightfully so,” said AMCC Director John McMillan in a statement. “Because of this, opening a dispensary is not an overnight process, but we appreciate the diligence of each of the licensees in moving forward with their plans to open first-class dispensaries across the state.”
At the program’s full capacity, there will be at least 37 dispensaries across the state, McMillan said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Newport’s Senate District 13 primary pits a progressive incumbent against a progressive challenger
description: At 47 years old with nine years in elected office, Sen. Dawn Euer is hardly the most seasoned lawmaker in a chamber where many members are retirees with multiple decades in their seats. But her Democratic primary opponent — her first since winning office in a 2017 special election —insists it’s time for fresh blood […]
text:
Charlene Lima, left, is challenging Sen. Dawn Euer, right, in the Democratic primary for Newport's Senate District 13. (Courtesy photos)
At 47 years old with nine years in elected office, Sen. Dawn Euer is hardly the most seasoned lawmaker in a chamber where many members are retirees with multiple decades in their seats.
But her Democratic primary opponent — her first since winning office in a 2017 special election —insists it’s time for fresh blood and fresh ideas in the seat representing Newport and Jamestown.
“I’ve heard no new ideas coming from the incumbent,” said Angela Lima, 45, who served three terms on the Newport City Council ending in 2024.


About Senate District 13
Represented by Sen. Dawn Euer since 2017
Geography: Newport, Jamestown 
Population: 27,542 residents, 16,034 registered voters 
Partisan breakdown: 48% independent, 40% Democrat, 12% Republican
Demographics: 41.6 median age, 78% white, $90,657 median household income (2024)


Yet the labor-endorsed challenger’s campaign focus on affordability and equity — in housing, education, healthcare and environmental sustainability — rings very similar to Euer’s.
Euer led legislation in many areas Lima says she wants to tackle. Euer sponsored the landmark decarbonization mandates of the 2021 Act on Climate Law, the 2022 Let RI Vote Act to expand voter access and ballot-casting methods, and a 2024 law protecting Rhode Island healthcare providers who provide reproductive and gender-affirming care from civil or criminal lawsuits from other states where these practices are not allowed. A private practice attorney and former chair of the Senate Committee on Judiciary, on which she still serves as a member, Euer was heavily involved in negotiations over high-profile gun safety legislation, and, during the 2026 session, the bill amending the statute of limitations on sexual abuse claims against institutions like the Roman Catholic Diocese of Providence that is now law.
“That’s something that’s helping real people, bringing justice to victims and helping people heal,” Euer said of the two-year window for otherwise time-barred sexual abuse claims to be filed. 
Even longer than her list of legislative wins is her to-do list. Euer named more protections for Rhode Island Energy ratepayers, preventing the company from recouping legal fees and repaving costs from customers, as two priorities she wants to bring back after her attempts were unsuccessful in 2026. 
She’s also guarded against attempts to weaken enforcement standards and penalties for landlords who fail to comply with registry and lead certification requirements meant to address childhood lead poisoning. A series of bills introduced, but not passed, in the 2026 legislative session would have reduced the requirements or weakened the penalties for noncompliant landlords.
Asked what policy differences she has with Euer, Lima repeated her own, three-pronged campaign message.
“My campaign is very simple: It is can you eat, are you safe, do you have somewhere to live?” she said.



Quotation







My campaign is very simple: It is can you eat, are you safe, do you have somewhere to live?


– Senate District 13 Democratic challenger Angela Lima 


Lima, who works as chief of government relations for the Women’s Fund of Rhode Island, is much clearer on her personal distinctions from Euer. A first-generation citizen, a queer, Black and Asian woman who bought her home in Newport’s North End with help from a first-time homebuyer assistance program via RIHousing, Lima sees herself as a better representation of the district’s diverse constituency.
“She ignores the most vulnerable,” Lima said of Euer, alleging the incumbent has been “unresponsive” to voters, herself included.
Euer refuted the allegations. 
“I’ve been working hard for my constituents to deliver results for the district,” she said, also defending her working-class background. “The experience I have is like the experience of so many Rhode Islanders, working more and more and not able to keep up.”
Euer rents a home in Newport’s Broadway neighborhood. She still has student loan debt, according to her 2025 financial disclosure form with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission.
Euer lives in Newport’s Broadway neighborhood. She still has student loan debt, according to her 2025 financial disclosure form with the Rhode Island Ethics Commission.
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, a Jamestown resident and Euer’s constituent, cited her outreach to the community as a strength. Euer is the only state legislative candidate to win Neronha’s endorsement.
“I really respect her work and her integrity,” Neronha said in an interview. “She is somebody that I turn to when I need outside reality checks on things like energy policy.”



Quotation







I’ve been working hard for my constituents to deliver results for the district.


– Sen. Dawn Euer, a Newport Democrat


Lima is among the 33 Democratic legislative candidates, most with contested primaries, backed by the influential Rhode Island AFL-CIO. The 80,000-member labor federation has supported Euer in the past, though not always with a formal endorsement, said Patrick Crowley, AFL-CIO president.
Crowley said Lima “represents the values of the labor movement,” but declined to elaborate.
Asked about her stance on the charter school moratorium signed into law by Gov. Dan McKee in June — a top priority for teachers unions — Lima, paused, asked for the question to be repeated, and then could only describe her general support for education and the public school system.
Despite not getting the AFL-CIO endorsement, Euer voted for the three-year ban on new charter schools.
Euer characterized the AFL-CIO’s endorsement of her primary opponent as “petty politics,” linked to a leadership feud in the upper chamber during late Senate President Dominick Ruggerio’s battle with cancer, and after his death in April 2025.
Crowley declined to comment. 
But Euer welcomed Lima as a challenger on the Sept. 9 ballot.
“I think everybody should have a challenger,” said Euer, who has run unopposed in every primary since the 2017 special election. “Competition is healthy. For me, it has helped me to be a better senator, to be better at campaigning.”
The winner of the primary is unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Who benefits from the ‘mansion tax’? Marylanders deserve to know
description: Taxes on high-end real estate are an increasingly popular way to raise funds for affordable housing units, writes J.H. Snider, but without data on who's actually benefiting, taxpayers can't know if the programs are paying off.
text:
Taxes on high-end real estate are an increasingly popular way to raise funds for affordable housing units, but data on who's actually benefiting from the programs is hard to come by. (Photo by Grace Cary/Getty stock photo)Maryland, like much of the nation, faces a severe housing affordability crisis. As the dream of homeownership slips out of reach for more families, political pressure has intensified for elected officials to deliver solutions. Among the proposed remedies, an increasingly favored mechanism is a local “wealth” or “mansion” tax.
Currently utilized by Baltimore City, Montgomery County and Anne Arundel County, these surcharges on high-value real estate transactions are designed to fund affordable housing via dedicated housing trust funds. As of 2024, 17 U.S. localities nationwide had implemented such a tax, with roughly half earmarking the revenue specifically for affordable housing.
In 2021, the General Assembly authorized Anne Arundel County to levy an additional 0.5% tax when a home sells for more than $1 million; in Baltimore City, the rate is 0.75%. Because this $1 million threshold is not indexed for inflation, its reach automatically expands. For perspective, $1 million in May 2021 holds the purchasing power of roughly $800,000 today. Furthermore, the tax applies to the entire value of the property, not just the amount exceeding the threshold. For a $1 million home carrying an $800,000 mortgage, the effective tax rate on actual home equity is 2.5% in Anne Arundel County and 3.75% in Baltimore City.
While framed as a progressive levy on luxury real estate, the secrecy surrounding these funds obscures how and to whom revenue is distributed. Because demand for housing subsidies vastly outstrips supply, long waiting lists are standard, giving program administrators and developers potential discretion to pick winners.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Do all eligible applicants stand an equal chance? To answer this, we must examine the data: What types of households actually win these subsidies, some worth hundreds of thousands of dollars?
Currently, Anne Arundel County tracks the race, ethnicity, and sex of recipients, but omits two critical economic indicators: income levels and employers. Obtaining this missing information is virtually impossible. The housing trust fund is administered by Arundel Community Development Services (ACDS), an entity exempt from Maryland’s Public Information Act. Furthermore, county officials maintain that individual applications from both homebuyers and developers are private, shielding them from public oversight.
This opacity undermines accountability. Proponents pitch these funds as lifelines for low-income households. In Anne Arundel County, the Area Median Income (AMI) for a four-person family is $133,500, with eligibility capped at 80% of AMI. (It is 100% of AMI for a newer Moderately Priced Dwelling Unit Program, which was lobbied for by school and county employees and mandates new developments with 10 or more units set aside 10% of them at below-market prices, effectively paid for by the nonsubsidized units.) Standard AMI calculations exclude benefit and pension compensation, which can raise effective compensation by over 50%. Without reporting on actual beneficiary incomes, the public cannot verify whether funds reach those in greatest need.
Even more troubling is the absence of employer data. Proponents argued the tax would attract and retain essential workers. Yet this priority is not codified in law or detailed in outcome reports. Without open records, the concern that these funds disproportionately benefit politically powerful groups such as public sector workers remains impossible to independently verify. The same reasoning applies to the Moderately Priced Dwelling Unit Program.
Politically, the tax structure minimizes immediate voter pushback. Because it is collected only at sale, current homeowners feel no immediate pain—often not until long after the enacting lawmakers have left office. Meanwhile, the low visibility of the program will facilitate the growing influence of the already two most politically powerful groups in local government: developers and government unions.
Ironically, by adding friction to real estate transactions, transfer taxes discourage older residents from downsizing. This locks up existing housing stock, constrains supply and inadvertently drives up prices—undermining the affordable housing policy’s stated goals.
To ensure public trust, housing trust funds must be subject to rigorous transparency, which entails sacrificing some recipient privacy.  As a compromise between transparency and privacy, anonymized income and employer data could be used, although at a significant cost to public oversight. Transitioning to open, machine-readable public data, which would eliminate the need for costly, slow, and often improperly denied public records requests, would ensure Maryland housing policy serves the broader public rather than political insiders.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Washtenaw judge tosses complaint against Ann Arbor Clerk over public power petition signatures
description: A Washtenaw County judge on Tuesday dismissed a case arguing the Ann Arbor City Clerk wrongly approved a ballot initiative that would set the city on a course to create a municipal electrical utility. The Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition filed a suit against City Clerk Jacqueline Beaudry and the city of Ann Arbor over […]
text:
Ann Arbor City Clerk's office. (Photo from Lilly Kujawski)A Washtenaw County judge on Tuesday dismissed a case arguing the Ann Arbor City Clerk wrongly approved a ballot initiative that would set the city on a course to create a municipal electrical utility.
The Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition filed a suit against City Clerk Jacqueline Beaudry and the city of Ann Arbor over Beaudry’s decision to certify petitions for the Ann Arbor for Public Power ballot proposal. 
If the proposal is approved, the city charter would be amended to create a municipal electric utility and set elections for its governing board for 2028. According to the ballot committee, DTE Energy, which currently supplies power to the city, would continue to provide electrical service until Ann Arbor residents vote to approve acquisition of local energy infrastructure in another referendum. 
DTE stands opposed to the proposal, citing an analysis it commissioned from the consulting firm Charles River Associates which places the up-front costs of a shift to municipal power at $1 billion. Ann Arbor for Public Power argues those costs are wildly inflated, and that the shift would carry benefits like more clean energy, lower rates and improved reliability.
According to reporting from Michigan Public, the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition — which is financially supported by DTE — argues that Ann Arbor for Public Power did not submit enough valid signatures to make the ballot, and that Beaudry had improperly allowed the group to submit additional sheets after her initial canvass.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group also argued that the ballot question includes more than one topic, in violation of the Home Rule City Act, which requires proposed charter amendments to focus on one subject.
However, Judge Patrick J. Conlin accepted the city’s request for summary disposition, determining Beaudry’s decision to accept signatures in batches was not a violation of the law and that she had acted in accordance with the Michigan Home Rule City Act.
In a statement shared with Michigan Advance, the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition expressed disappointment with Conlin’s decision.
“Michigan law sets strict, clear rules for how ballot petitions must be gathered and filed, and we continue to believe those rules were not followed here,” said Rudy Harper, the group’s spokesperson. “The stakes — a proposed city takeover of the electric grid carrying an estimated $1 billion in new debt — demand a petition process that meets the letter of the law.”
The group has since appealed.
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Ann Arbor City Attorney Atleen Kaur said, “We are pleased that the Court correctly recognized the Clerk’s canvass was compliant with the Home Rule City Act.” She noted that the city will evaluate the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition’s appeal and respond accordingly. 
Ann Arbor for Public Power cheered Conlin’s decision.
“Ann Arbor residents want their electric bill payments to fund grid maintenance and renewable power, not corporate profits and baseless lawsuits,” said Brian Geiringer, the group’s executive director. “We look forward to making the case for public power this fall.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: The number of Denver overdose deaths is shocking. The city is making it worse.
description: Aug. 31 is Overdose Grief Day, when people impacted by the preventable and devastating overdose crisis come together to acknowledge all those who have experienced an overdose, the lives we have lost, as well as loved ones and others affected. For the last two years, nearly two people die every day from an overdose right […]
text:
A Drug Enforcement Administration vest and mask sit on a table. Denver Police and the DEA announced “Operation Overdose Intercept” that will send a surge of law enforcement into communities. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)Aug. 31 is Overdose Grief Day, when people impacted by the preventable and devastating overdose crisis come together to acknowledge all those who have experienced an overdose, the lives we have lost, as well as loved ones and others affected.
For the last two years, nearly two people die every day from an overdose right here in Denver. These numbers are shocking and painful, not only because of the loss of human life, but because each one of those deaths could have been prevented. There are proven methods to prevent overdose such as overdose prevention centers, ending stigma, access to healthcare and distribution of Naloxone. Public health and community care can end overdose.
Instead, the city of Denver has renewed its dedication to the racist and classist “war on drugs.” One week before Overdose Grief Day, Denver Police and the Drug Enforcement Agency announced “Operation Overdose Intercept” that will send a surge of law enforcement into communities continuing failed tactics that hurt people and fail to address overdose.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a moment where vulnerable communities like immigrants, unhoused and transgender people are living in fear of federal attacks, Denver is choosing to bring more federal agents into Denver. At a time where the city is unable to fund essential programs and positions it will hemorrhage money into arrests and incarceration — an approach that has been demonstrated to fail at reducing drug use or preventing overdose. With the knowledge that people released from jail are dramatically more likely to overdose, Denver will be funneling more people into the overcrowded jails. It’s no secret that overdoses have surged in our county jail and now it appears to be the state’s largest detox center.
This calloused and deadly path will have consequences. Those consequences will have names, friends, families and communities. The people who will suffer — predominantly Black, Brown, Indigenous, and people of color; poor; working class; unhoused; 2SLBTQIA+; and otherwise marginalized — will pay the price both in increased policing and more devastating loss.
As families and friends take a moment to grieve those that we have lost on Monday, the city of Denver continues to double down on incarceration and criminalization which will only serve to increase overdose deaths. It is time to stop the hamster wheel of failed policy and look at what truly works.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: With regulations approved, freestanding birth centers near a reality in Kentucky
description: LOUISVILLE — After more than half a decade of advocacy, supporters of freestanding birth centers celebrated Thursday as a legislative committee approved regulations — essentially, the details — for how the centers will now be able to open and run.  Mary Kathryn DeLodder, the director of the Kentucky Birth Coalition who has long advocated for […]
text:
Mary Kathryn DeLodder, the director of the Kentucky Birth Coalition who has long advocated for more birthing options in the state, speaks about freestanding birth centers on Thursday, August 27, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd) LOUISVILLE — After more than half a decade of advocacy, supporters of freestanding birth centers celebrated Thursday as a legislative committee approved regulations — essentially, the details — for how the centers will now be able to open and run. 
Mary Kathryn DeLodder, the director of the Kentucky Birth Coalition who has long advocated for more birthing options in the state, doesn’t have a timeline yet on when Kentucky may have its first center, but said she’s already heard from several people interested in opening them. 
The regulations — which had to be brought up to date since no freestanding birthing center has operated in Kentucky in decades — are “going to really allow for birth centers to come into the modern times and operate in the commonwealth,” DeLodder said.  
“I’m excited for Kentucky families that are experiencing low risk low risk pregnancies to have access to freestanding birth centers as another maternity care option,” she said, “and I’m also thankful for the hospitals that will be working cooperatively with these centers to continue to serve mothers and babies who have more complex needs.” 
Freestanding birth centers are closing as maternity care gaps grow

In 2025 the legislature paved the way for freestanding birth centers to open in Kentucky after years of debate over the merits and safety of the centers, which are home-like facilities aimed toward low-risk pregnancies. 
The key hurdle that long blocked the centers from opening in Kentucky — which was removed by the 2025 law — was the state’s requirement that they obtain a certificate of need, which is a process that attempts to certify that there is a need for a service, be that extra beds in a hospital, an extra MRI machine or a new facility altogether. 
Kentucky, meanwhile, has poor statistics around maternity care: Too many babies are born preterm and the rate of mothers dying in and around childbirth is higher than the national average, to name a few. 
DeLodder said while freestanding birthing centers can’t solve all of these problems, “it will help to have more options” for the parents in Kentucky who want them. 
And the demand has long been there. The Lantern has reported through the years that hundreds of Kentuckians travel out of state in order to give birth at freestanding birth centers. 
“We know people want this because they are willing to go out of state. But if you live multiple hours away in the middle of Kentucky, then crossing the state line to go to a freestanding center isn’t an option,” she said. “Because we’ve seen the advocates and families stick with this initiative and push it for six years, I think that shows the dedication that people have to wanting to see this happen.” 
Rep. Jason Nemes, who for years fought to make freestanding birth centers a reality in Kentucky, said the state is “in the right spot … for Kentucky families, and most importantly, for mothers and babies.” 
“This,” he said, “has been a long day coming.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: If Va.’s reproductive rights amendment passes, challengers say they’ll fight to overturn it in court
description: A legal challenge to amend the ballot language for Virginia’s pending reproductive rights constitutional amendment has been in limbo since June. Even if no movement on the case happens before Election Day, counsel for the plaintiffs said this week, they will seek to invalidate the vote.  Josh Hetzler, a lawyer with the Founding Freedoms Law […]
text:
An attendee of the Virginia March For Life on April 22, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)A legal challenge to amend the ballot language for Virginia’s pending reproductive rights constitutional amendment has been in limbo since June. Even if no movement on the case happens before Election Day, counsel for the plaintiffs said this week, they will seek to invalidate the vote. 
Josh Hetzler, a lawyer with the Founding Freedoms Law Center said, “If the amendment passes, we would seek to be in court as soon as possible to ask the court to overturn the result, similar to how it happened with the redistricting amendment.”
Virginians approved another amendment to redraw congressional maps in a special election that the Supreme Court of Virginia struck down weeks later — an outcome Hetzler would push for if voters accept the reproductive health amendment.  
The lawsuit, first filed in April on behalf of Bluefield town council member Meagan Kade and Chesterfield County child psychologist Sheila Furey, calls the ballot language for the amendment misleading and seeks it to be rewritten or the amendment invalidated. 
The last hearing about it was in June in Tazewell (where the redistricting lawsuit also originated). An advocacy group called Virginians For Reproductive Freedom has tried to join the case as a co-defendant. 
As of Aug. 27, no ruling has been issued. 
Hetzler said “the Commonwealth, from our standpoint, has been dragging its feet and has not tried to schedule a hearing for its motions to dismiss our case.” 
The office of Attorney General Jay Jones and Tazewell Circuit Court did follow through on inquiries about when a hearing could next take place. 
 What the case has sought

In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs said the ballot language for the referendum “profoundly misleads by omission and misrepresentation.” 

The proposed amendment reads:
“Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient’s health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?”

Plaintiffs argued the amendment would eliminate parental consent requirements for minors to receive abortions or surgical birth control procedures and pose safety risks by removing the current three-physician approval threshold for abortions that happen later in pregnancy. 
The arguments mirror objections voiced by Republican lawmakers at each step of the amendment’s multi-year approval process so far. 
Existing state code requires parental or guardian consent for surgeries on minors, unless a minor successfully petitions a judge for approval. 
Democrats, who hold legislative majority and advanced the amendment to statewide ballots, responded by saying it wouldn’t override state law and instead would more firmly protect access to abortion, contraception and fertility treatment. 
A remedy for this argument, Hetzler suggested at an April press conference, would be a rewrite of the amendment’s language before early voting begins on Sep. 18. 
“We’re saying ‘declare that if this language goes forward, that it would be unconstitutionally deceptive, and it could therefore be declared void after the fact,’” Hetzler later said in a call. 
With a declaratory judgement, the legislature “would have every incentive to try to fix the language,” he explained, suggesting a special session could be called to “make it more accurate to what the amendment actually does.”
 Other avenues for defeat

Another argument in the Family Foundation case challenged whether the retroactive repeal of contradictory state code outlining additional constitutional amendment requirements was legal. 
That case was first filed in March by Bedford County supervisor Charla Bansley  and dismissed in July. Bansley has since filed an appeal. 
More than abortion: What Va. patients and providers want you to know about reproductive health laws

The repealed code that would have required circuit court clerks post amendment text outside their courthouses — § 30-13 — conflicted with another part of state code outlining the process, which lacked that specific requirement. 
When Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed bills to hold a referendum for the amendments earlier this year, she also signed a bill to repeal § 30-13.
Because the Family Foundation’s case also includes arguments involving § 30-13, Hetzler suggests it may lend credence to the Liberty Counsel case. The argument also surfaced in the successful challenge to the redistricting amendment, though it was not the focal point of the Supreme Court’s ruling. 
Ahead of the Liberty Counsel case’s dismissal, lawyers debated Article 12, Section 1 of Virginia’s Constitution — which outlines the state legislature’s responsibility to submit pending amendments to voters “in such manner as it shall prescribe.”
Because the constitutional amendment occurred while § 30-13 was still on the books, Bansley and her attorneys said the process should be invalidated. 
Though the repeal did not take effect until this summer, Erin McNeil with the state’s attorney general office said lawmakers have authority to adjust the constitution and prescribe how they do it. 
“How can the General Assembly have this authority to prescribe a process but not have the authority to change that process?” she asked.
A Campbell County judge ruled from the bench that day in favor of the state.But with the appeal filed, it could be revived. 
Liberty Counsel founder Mat Staver said in a release that the case “will ultimately be determined by Virginia’s highest courts.”
While it’s unclear if pro-amendment advocacy group Virginians For Reproductive Freedom can get involved in the Family Foundation case or whether another hearing may occur before Election Day, the group was granted intervention in the Liberty Counsel case. 
VRF campaign manager Han Jones called the appeal “desperate” and said the organization is confident the dismissal could stand because “decisions about Virginia’s Constitution belong to the people.”

title: As student well-being concerns grow, Va. advocates push for stricter school tech guidelines
description: Former educators and parents say Virginia leaders must implement guidelines to regulate the digital tools students use in schools, arguing that technology is obscuring the essential learning methods they need most. Virginia parents and educators are urging leaders, including the Board of Education, to reduce excessive classroom screen time by considering a d[...]
text:
Virginia parents and educators are urging leaders, including the Board of Education, to reduce excessive classroom screen time by considering a draft policy that prioritizes distraction-free learning, physical books, writing, and face-to-face interaction. (Photo by Daniel de la Hoz/Getty Images)Former educators and parents say Virginia leaders must implement guidelines to regulate the digital tools students use in schools, arguing that technology is obscuring the essential learning methods they need most.
Virginia parents and educators are urging leaders, including the Board of Education, to reduce excessive classroom screen time by considering a draft policy that prioritizes distraction-free learning, physical books, writing, and face-to-face interaction.
The effort comes as schools continue leaning heavily on technology, which has ramped up since the COVID-19 pandemic shut down in-person school instruction five years ago and later reopened, leaving learning gaps that state lawmakers and educators have struggled to address.
Virginia Screen-Free Week encourages you to unplug for a bit

Keena McAvoy, mother and co-founder of DMV Unplugged, a nonprofit focused on reducing kids’ use of smartphones and other technology, said she and others are uncertain what the Virginia Department of Education knows about how technology is being used in schools.
“I don’t think there’s a clear picture of what exactly is happening in schools with technology and … that’s the problem with not having a policy or some sort of acknowledgment of what’s actually happening,” McAvoy said, citing concerns about students accessing graphic material on school devices, playing games and avoiding interactions with classmates. 
DMV Unplugged is working alongside Virginia parents, educators, and organizations such as The Balance Project and Distraction Free Schools Policy Project to raise awareness of the issue and push for the policy shifts in the commonwealth.
These groups say digital products should support learning, privacy, and safety, but not risk students’ well-being or use children to make a profit. Many of them spoke at the Board of Education’s business meeting on Thursday.
Cameron Hardesty, a mother of three in Albemarle County, urged the board to drastically reduce or eliminate screen use for young children in schools. She criticized her local school for its heavy reliance on technology and “buzz breaks” for kindergartners, arguing that early, frequent device use makes children “more anxious, more distracted, (and) unable to sustain attention long enough to develop the critical thinking skills they need.”
Amber Rhodes, a former educator and leader with The Balance Project, which promotes balancing a healthy lifestyle and the use of technology, said her colleagues are seeking to support schools and help teachers “do what they do best,” which is teaching.
Rhodes spent eight years as a middle school teacher, with her last year spent serving as an innovative learning coach, helping teachers integrate technology into their classroom lessons.
“I really felt like my first few years of teaching was kind of what we’re trying to get back to … that good pedagogical practice of building relationships with the students, hands-on students exploring… all of those things that we know are good teaching, but the devices have sort of gotten in the way,” Rhodes said. 
 Proposed policy

Organizers and advocates are proposing a policy package that would establish statewide minimum standards to ensure that digital tools used by students are appropriate, approved and used properly in public schools. 
The draft policy would create a statewide framework for approving and overseeing digital products used in public schools. 
General Assembly passes bill giving schools more say on classroom phone rules

Additionally, the proposal would give students and caregivers the right to opt out of the use of digital products as part of a student’s education. The measure would also protect teachers if they choose to teach without electronic devices.
Beginning in July 2024, former Gov. Glenn Youngkin signed an executive order to push the commonwealth toward phone-free schools. Subsequently, lawmakers passed legislation giving local school boards more control over how those restrictions are implemented.
 What’s next

Sen. Schyler VanValkenburg, D-Henrico, confirmed this week that he will introduce a model policy on the use of educational technology and digital products for the upcoming General Assembly session beginning in January.
The goal, he said, is to start a conversation about the purposeful use of technology and when and where it may be appropriate to minimize its use, as artificial intelligence, social media, video content and other technologies have increasingly been integrated into people’s lives.
Rhodes was one of many parents who spoke in support of the proposed policy at the board’s business meeting. 
The research is very new,” Rhodes said.  “I think Virginia leaders are going to have to take a look at the research and make a decision about what they think is best based on what’s happening in the classrooms and the research that we have at this point.”

title: With six West Nile cases reported statewide, infected mosquitos are on the rise in Virginia Beach
description: By Yiqing Wang/WHRO West Nile virus is showing up in Virginia Beach mosquitoes at a level the city’s biologist says she has not seen in four years. Virginia has reported six human cases so far this year, including one in the Eastern Region, though Virginia Beach officials said Aug. 19 that no human cases had been reported […]
text:
A female Culex quinquefasciatus mosquito on the skin of a human host. Virginia Beach has detected high West Nile virus activity in local mosquito samples this season.(James Gathany/ Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)By Yiqing Wang/WHRO
West Nile virus is showing up in Virginia Beach mosquitoes at a level the city’s biologist says she has not seen in four years.
Virginia has reported six human cases so far this year, including one in the Eastern Region, though Virginia Beach officials said Aug. 19 that no human cases had been reported in the city.
But the city has detected the virus in 50 mosquito pools collected from 24 locations this season. In each of the previous two or three seasons, only one or two pools tested positive.
“This is a high year for us,” said Kaitlyn Price, a mosquito biologist with the Virginia Beach Public Works Mosquito Control program. “I don’t think that I have tested this many mosquitoes at this point in the season in my four years of being here.”
A mosquito pool is a group of mosquitoes collected from the same trap and tested together. Price said some traps caught so many Culex mosquitoes, the main carrier of West Nile virus, that the mosquitoes had to be divided into several pools.
Despite the sharp increase in positive mosquito pools, Price said the results do not mean human cases will rise at the same rate.
“We’ve had years where we’ve had way more mosquitoes and no disease activity,” Price said.
Mosquito populations can rise or fall with temperature, rainfall and the availability of standing water.
Most people infected with West Nile virus do not develop symptoms. Some experience fever, body aches, vomiting, diarrhea or a rash.
Rare cases can cause severe neurological illness or death, with older adults and people with weakened immune systems facing greater risk.
Price said Virginia Beach places about 90 mosquito traps across the city each week. Workers collect the traps, identify the mosquito species and test pools of species known to carry disease.
This year, the city has tested more than 300 pools for West Nile virus and Eastern equine encephalitis, another viral disease spread by the bites of infected mosquitoes.
When a pool tests positive, crews increase surveillance and apply larvicide to standing water in the surrounding area. The treatment kills mosquitoes before they develop into flying, biting adults.
“It’s much more effective to control mosquitoes while they’re in the larval stage because they spend three quarters of their life there versus when they’re adults and actively flying and biting,” Price said.
Price said the city also uses nighttime spraying when monitoring shows high mosquito numbers or continued virus activity.
The Virginia Beach Department of Public Health is notifying residents and explaining how they can reduce their exposure, said Rob Robinson, the department’s environmental health program manager.
Robinson urged residents to empty water from flowerpots, birdbaths, clogged gutters, children’s toys and other containers that can become breeding sites. He also recommended using insect repellent and wearing long sleeves and pants between dusk and dawn.
“The best preventive measure to avoid the virus is to avoid being bitten in the first place,” Robinson said.
